AN EVIL EXANPLE.—I must say a little on one, unfor- tunately, but too prevalent phase of evil example on the part of parents, and that is the carelessness in speech, more especially when it refers to our neighbours, which some people are in the habit of exhibiting almost every day of their lives. I have in my mind a certain family in which this pernicious habit was indulged, and nearly every one of the children only too faithfully reproduced in their lives the models of the originals. Nothing was too sacred to escape their censure or ridicule; the neigh- bours were subjected to every species of criticism. Not a single idiosincracy was spared. Ruthlessly it was thrown into the crucible and as ruthlessly subjected to analysis, and the unvarying result was unpitying laugh- ter, impish scorn, or unconcealed sneers. Why should I continue the picture, save to add that all this much-to- be-pitied family grew up to be despised and spurned by all right-minded people? LEECHES AT Laitoa.—ln the carriage of the night ex- press train from Vienna to Berlin, the passengers were recently aroused from their sleep by the loud shrieks of a lady, who asserted that there was "a murderer in the carriage." The passengers, who could get no other answer from her but a declaration that she was being stabbed with sharp instruments in several places, called the guard. She would not submit to an examination, and the guard was at his wits end what to do, when a stout gentleman roared out that he, too, was being pricked cruelly in various parts of his thigh. The gen- tleman was at the next station searched, and six large leeches were discovered to be feasting themselves upon his leg. The lady had swooned from fright and weak- ness. One of the passengers had brought an insuffi- ciently covered jar of these blood-suckers into the car- riage, and had placed it upon the seat. They escaped, and did the mischief. THE ZENANA ON THE BATTL.E-FIELD.—The moment the lines confronted each other on changing their ground, Hyder suspected the day was lost, and requested the Nizam to get the guns into the redoubts and defend the fortified position; but the Nizam, furious with rage and mortification, refused the advice, and declined to quit the field till he saw tho steady British line coming on, firing as it advanced, ere; the bayonets would come flash- ing down to the charge. According to his general wont, he had all his favourite wives in the field, or near it, in gilded and cumbersome howdahs on the backs of elephants, and with the order that the artillery should retire, he added that the zenana should also fall back; but from one of the howdahs a dark-skinned damsel called aloud, " This elephant has not been taught to turn —it only follows the standard of the empire !" The odalisque made good her wish, nor did her unwieldy bearer turn his tail to the foe till the standard had passed to the rear. By that time our bullets were flying among the gorgeous howdahs, and many were stricken for whom they never were intended. Our troops ad- vanced to the charge, and then the whole gave way be- fore them, and, abandoning everything, the cowardly Nizam, at the head of a body of chosen horse, fled towards the west, nor halted Ulf he had left the gorges of the Chingama Pass behind him.—From " Cassell's Illustrated History of India" for December. 1 BED-MAKING UNDER THE TITDOIIS.—A curious' account I has been preserved—in a MS. by Peter •le Neve, Norroy King-at-Arms—of the way in which the bed of Henry VII. was made in his palaces of Shene and elsewhere. It is so much to our purpose that it may be quoted here. From his time court ceremonial, and perhaps it may be said in general, modern manners were brought under some kind of definite rules. The old feudal system came to an end on Bosworth Field. Old families had been destroyed or decimated by the civil wars. Henceforth kings were supreme. Rennaissance manners were in full swing all over Europe. This is the way his Majesty's bed was to be made— The curtains must be drawn (the spelling is modernised), and a gentleman usher must hold the curtains together; then must two squires of the body stand at the bed's head, and two yeomen of the Crown at the bed's feet, and all the stuff laid safe at the bed's .feet on a carpet till the contents of the palliasse (which was cpen in the middle) were re-made. Then a yeotnan to leap upon the bed and roll him up and down and ar- ray the litter; then to lay down the canvas again, then the feather bed, and beat it well and make it even and smooth Then take the fustian (under blanket) and cast it upon the bed without any wrinkles, and the sheet in the same wise." Then follow directions regarding the sheet, how it is to be stroked smooth, tucked under the feather bed, over it is to be laid " Vother stuff," upper sheet blankets, and fustian, and over that a covering of martin's fur and ermine. "A yeoman to beat the pil- lows and throw them up to the squires to lay them on the bed head, as.pleaseth the King's grace." A sheet of Rennes was passed under the pillows, falling over loose in front (no pillow case), over that a rug of ermine. The bed clothes were then to be brought well up to the pil- lows and turned down the space of an ell. It is added ,that when all was done, these functionaries withdrew behind the curtain that divided the room and had a drink all round.—./. Huteyerford Pullen, in "The Magazine of Art."

A RACE AGAINST DEATE.—Perhaps I had slept an hour, possibly not so long, when I woke up choking with salt water and slushy ice-paste—a wild struggle, the flinging up of arms and then the spike-charged waters rushed from my head while I gasped for life,, the wave poured along the passage into the saloon, breaking in doors, tossing the skipper's harmonium like an orange from end to end until the sides parted, and the keys floated loosely amongst other waste. I made up a portion of that drift- waste as I pitched aimlessly about, and mixed with the mashed potatoes and dissolving flour, or, watched other potatoes, not yet mashed, Careering along the tables like billiard-balls, while plates, cruet-stands, salt-cellars, and wine-glasses, possessed of animation, rushed recklessly to destruction. As I saw all this, and then turned to where the swarthy Aberdonian skipper rolled down the companion steps, squinting horribly at the severed key- board • and floating pieces of his pet instrument and friend of lonely sea hours, I felt the drowning of the galley fires was not the last stroke of sullen Fate. Pick up the bits, lads," he groaned wearily, "and you, painter-chap, come on deck if you want to see a wave." This title referred to me, and as the planks were becom- ing somewhat firmer under foot, I groped the.best of my way after the skipper, to where three seamen were clings mg to. rather than controlling, the wheel Behind them reared a dense black precipice of solid water, beetling cliffs which rose far over our heads, seeming to rise over the top of the mainmast, straight as a wall, with ti coping at the head, rushing after us like the Scotch ex- press, growing every instant bigger, bending every in- Stant farther, casting its great shadow—the dark shadow of death—along the poop, main-deck, and portion of the forecastle, leaving only the straining sheets and bulging sails at the bow glittering like three flakes of.'snow in the ghastly sunshine. We were "head-reaching," run- ning a stern race against death. All our hopes rested in those two narrow strips of swollen, shadow-darkened canvas on our foretop and maintop sail-yards, with the three shining ribbons at the bow. If these split, fare- well to life and England, for thousands of tonszvill fall and crush us to atoms in one instant, without leaving a whole plank to tell the fate of the Christiana in that piti- less A.ntarctic Ocean. Sliding gradually down the Aides of that black mountain, we raced over it,, while it gal- loped madly under us, a mountain smooth aff gassed or fused asphalte from its own velocity, with the surge steadfast upen its breast, and the ice-lumps and spike- ends pointing steadfastly towards the base, each lump and foam-curd reflected like our weather-worn hull within the darkness down to the gulf before us—that gulf of boiling, whirling spume.—From " Cassell's Fan,ily Magazine" for December. I ONLY CRIED WITH HER. "My darling, it IS bedtime; come and kneel By me, and say your prayers: but tell me anti Mat kindly act, or deed, throughout the day g You have performed." The little maiden bent ' 6 Her head in silence for awhile, and said, "I do not know of any. When I found - That little Jenny had returned to school After the absence of a week, and saw Her eyelids red with weeping, I inquired The cause: she burst into a flood of tears: And when I saw she could not speak, I took . Her little hand in mine and wept with her. • After a while she told me, 'midst her sobs, That her dear brother, whom she loved so wall . And nursed so tenderly, had suffered much, I Growing still weaker; till at length he died, 7 And that she never, never could forgetl His thin, pale face, as on the couch he lay. Too weak for speech. but speaking with his eyes Of love unchangeable. And when she knelt % Beside him, he had clasped her hand, and pressed 'Her fingers to his pallid lips and died. And that they took his lifeless form away And laid it in the grave; and never more Would she behold his loving face again. And then she wept as if her heart would break I could net speak to her, but put my face Against her cheek, and kept her company. After awhile she wiped her eyes, and threw Her arms around my neck and kissed me twioe, And said she felt much better, that my tears Had done her good; and that is all I know." : With what delight the mother heard her child Thus modestly describe how she had wept With her afflicted schoolfellow. How true It is, that, for a deeply-wounded heart, The best cure is the balm of sympathy-, Then deem it not an idle thing to speak . A loving word to brethren in distress. The very face you wear, the smile you give, May heal a breaking heart, and drive away Corroding care, and spread fresh life and joy Where else had been distress and misery. .--Leeds Weekly Mercury. J. R. Ronusson.

Eating dates is a pleasant way of killing time. "Physic," says an old surgeon, "is the art of amusing the patient, while Nature cures the disease." ' Mr. More wrote to a girl asking her to marry him. She declined, and closed her note with—" No more at present" He is a very ordinary man who never finds fault with himself, and a very extraordinary one who never has reason to do so. Why is a foolish fellow in a high station like a man in a balloon? Because everybody appears little to him and he appears little to everybody.. Teacher: "Who reigned latter Saul?" Little Bessie: "David." "And who came after David?" "Solomon." "And who came after Solomon?" "The Queen of Sheba." A rather prosy old gentleman, accustomed to interlard his disoourse with long outlandish words, used to say that on one occasion he jumped laconically over a ditch, meaning that he did it straight away and without hesi- tation. _

Guest : "Walter, did you say this was genuine turtle soup ?" Waiter: "Yes, sir. It was made out of the water of a pond near here in which a turtle was seen last summer. A physician says: "If a child does not thrive on fresh milk, boil it." Ho doesn't state how long the child should be boiled. We should think there would be dan- ger in leaving it to boil too long. The latest precocious saying is by an infant. She had torn one of her nails to the quick, and going to her mother, while the pain filled her eyes with tears, said, holding up her wounded finger, "Mamma, I dess I shall have to go up to heaven and dit anozzer put on:" An Irishman who had been doing some work for a clergyman was asked to take a dram. After he drank it, he looked at the glass, and said, "Can your honour tell me how they make thim glasses so nate?" The clergyman gave him the information how glass was blown. "Atrial sure, thin," said Paddy," he must have been moighty short i' the wind that blew that glass." An American Justice of the Peace, who is constantly trying criminal cases, was called on to marry a couple. After he had asked the usual question if they desired to be united in the bonds of matrimony, and they had re- plied in the affirmative, the Justice said solemnly— Having pleaded guilty to the charge, if there are in your opinion any mitigating circumstances, now is the time to state what they are.' Examiner: "What is the colour of this flag?" Engi- neer: "Green, sir." "Right. Now close your left eye. What is the colour of this flag?" "Orson, sir. Dark green." "Just so. Shut you right eye. What flag am I waving now?" "A black one, sir." "Nonsense. It's bright red. And this flag ?" "Black, sir." " Pshaw ! It is white. Your left eye seems ..a little off." "Well,

may be it is. It is a glass eye, sir." An excellent remark of Judge Maule's has been so often repeated that we almost fear to "dish it up again." Maule," said a somewhat vain although profoundly learned Judge, speaking to our witty friend as he was quietly taking his lunch of bread and cheese in the Judge's private room, " Maule, why do you drink beer ?" "To bring my mind down' to a level with the other Judges," was the immediate reply. A half-famished fellow tells of a baker whose loaves had been growing smaller by degrees and beautifully less, who, when going on his round to serve his custo- mers, stopped at the door of one of them and knocked. The lady within exclaimed—" Who's there ?" and was answered "The baker." "What do you want ?" "To leave your bread." "Well, you needn't make such a fuss about it; put it through the keyhole." Curran conversing with Sir Thos. Turton, happened to remark that he could never speak in public for a quarter of an hour without moistening his lips; to which Sir Thomas replied that, in that respect, he had the advan- tage of him :—" I spoke," said he, "the other night in the House of Commons for five hours, on the Nabob of Oude, and never felt in the least thirsty." "It is very remark- able, indeed," rejoined Curran, "for everyone agrees that it was the driest speech of the session." A NARROW Escepe.—A singular story, which refers to Uxbridge, is told by Mr. H. Fynes Clinton respecting his great-great-grandiather, one Norreys Fynes, alias Clinton. Be was in the Royalist army under Charles 1.,' and was taken prisoner at Northampton; but Prince Rupert having captured a man of importance, a Mr. Wright, of Uxbridge, an exchange of prisoners was ar- ranged, and the trumpeter announcing this exchange arrived in the Market-phice at Uxbridge just as the rope had been put round and the last Psalm or hymn was being sung, at the end of which he was to be turned off. Thus the existence of a large collateral branch of the ducal family of Newcastle for some minutes depetided on the length to which a Psalm was drawled out C,~ll's "Greaser Landon" for December.

MAMTKRB AT Ho3rs.-1. Shut every door after you without slamming it. 2. Never stamp, run, or jump in the house. 3. Never call to persons upstairs or in the next room; if you wish to speak to them, go quietly where they are. 4. Always speak kindly and politely to the servants, if you would have them do the same to you. 5. When told to do or not to do a thing by either parent, never ask why you should or should not. 6. Tell of your own faults, but not those of your brothers and sisters. 7. Carefully clean the mud or snow from your boots or shoes before entering the house. 8. Be Prompt at every meal. 9. Never sit down at the table or in the parlour with dirty hands or tumbled hair. 10. Never interrupt any conversation, but wait patiently for your turn to speak. 11. Never reserve your good man- ners for strangers, but be eqhally polite at home and abroad. 12. Avoid slang.. HE TOOL Tax OTHRM.—A gentleman who raid the best prices for his provisions and who liked to hire as well as did his neighbours, was once deceived by his poulterer in the age of some poultry he bought. Meeting the dealer a few days afterwards, he walked up to his wag- gon and inquired, "Got any geese to-day ?" "0 yes," said the poulterer. "a fine lot.' "How many have you got?" "A dozen—nice ones." The customer then turned them over, and then he added, "Now, you see, I've got a pesky lot of fellows at my house, an' they eat a great deal Of Poultry. Haven't you got any tough ones?" "Well, yes," said the dealer, picking them over. "There's one, two, three, four, five of 'em." "Is that all the tough ones you've got?" '‘‘ Yes, yes; that's all," said the dealer separating them. "Well, then, I reckon on the whole, continued the buyer, "I'll take the other lot" The poul- terer looked thoughtful, and, like most thoughtful people, was silent.—Youth's Compitaion.

As instrument for ascertaining the distances of aeoea- sibie and of inaccessible objects has been invented by Dr. Luigi Cerebotani, of Verona. The apparatus con- sists of a pair of telescopes mounted on a stand, and , fixed on a tripod for use. The telescopes are both, brought to bear on the object, and a reading of their an- gular position is then taken from a graduated scale on. the instrument, which, compared with a set of priated tables, gives the distance; the necessity for laying down a base-line as usual being thus dispensed with. Dis- tances can also be measured between distant objects, and a rough plan of the country observed can be sketched. In the same way the distance of ships at sea , can be determined. A New TELHPRONR 5T911331 FOR Movnto Tams.--Por some tine past there has been in course of construction, on the narrow-gauge line between Paw Paw sad Lawton, Michigan, a telephone line, by means of which a moving train can be put in communication with stations in either direction, or with other moving trains. The line is now completed, and the trials made are reported tobe satisfactory. The poles holding the wire are all placed near the track, and at equal distance from it. On each • pole at a height of 12 feet above the rails an arm extends towards the track. On the upper side of this arm stand the small iron clamps that hold the wire. A gas pipe standard is erected upon the cab of the engine reaching up to a point level with the wire. From thie standard 'there extend two stationary arms one reaching forward, and one backward. A cap made to turn either right or left fits upon the top of this standard. TO this cap is attached by a hinge joint the long Iron arm which rests upon the wire. This arm reaches beyond the stan- dard, and the exeass of weight on the one side is balanced by a spring upon the other, so that but a few ounces of weight rest upon the wire. From the short arms before described, two springs of equal strength extend to the long arm, holding it at right angles to the track. An in- sulated wire is soldered to the long arm and brought down through the hollow standard into the cab. From there it runs into a car, and is attached to an ordinary Bell telephone, the engine or the trucks of the car being used as earth. It was [seared that them might not prove a good earth connection, but the experiments made give good results. One other question had to be tested by trial, namely, whether the contact of a rod moving swiftly along the wire would be steady enough to trans- mit an even current. The working of the apparatus de- scribed is said to have preyed so satisfactory as to sur- prise the most sanguine. Conversation in the cars, while running at a rapid rate, was held with the stations on either side with no more difficulty than between two or- dinary telephone stations.—lron. FIRBPROOP PAPBR Sveucrunas.—The Japanese are imitating Europeans in clothing and many other customs and ideas, and in turn we are learning from them and imitating some of their peculiar usages. One of the most remarkable of these is the application of paper to a multitude of purposes. Engineering describes a chimney built entirely of paper by a manufacturer of Breslau. It is 50 feet in height, and constructed of blocks of compressed paper, joined together by silicious cement. It is said to be very elastic and fireproof. Its elasticity and lightness will not be questioned, but many will be disposed to doubt that it is fireproof. In reference to this I may state my own experience. A number of un- bound sheets of "The Fuel of the Sun" were stored at a bookbinder's warehouse at the time of a disastrous fire, and I took it for granted that they were consumed. The salvage of such material bearing. so ominous a title ap- peared hopeless, nevertheless, I visited the premises and made inquiry. I found that although the package of sheets standing on the shelves had been freely exposed to the flames only a few, those at the top, were seriously damaged, and such was the case with other similar packages. The exposed edges of the sheets were burned only to a small depth. In many cases the effect was little more than a trimming of margins by burning away the irregularly projecting edges. The difficulty of burning through a well-compressed mass of paper, even sheets, is curiously great, and when made into solid blocks its resistance must of course be much greater. Although wood is far more porous and much more easily burned than such paper, it is found that a stout oaken beam stands in a raging fire far longer than an iron girder. If two similar houses ware built, one of paper-blocks painted over with a silicious coating, and the other with brick, the internal fittings and contents being alike in both, and both were " gutted " by fire, I have no doubt that the paper walls would stand far better than the brick walla. The latter would give way, partly on account of their weight and the disintegration of the mortar, while the paper would reinain internally unaltered, merely charred superficially. Paper as a building and furnishing material has yet a great future before it. If I were only half as mad as the majority of the twenty thousand victims who annually immolate their capital in securing and trying to carry out patents. I should rush at once to the Great Seal Office and ob- tain a monopoly for the construction of fireproof paper safes, to supersede the iron safes now so largely used. DISAPPHARANCH OF AN ISLAND.—An official notifica- Hon from the Danish Ministry of Marine announces that Denmark is poorer by the loss of an island and of an in- teresting natural object. South of the Island of Suderoe, one of the Faroe group, a mighty cliff rose sheer out of the sea to a height of from 80ft. to 100 ft. Looked at sidewise from a distance at sea, it resembled a great ship ih full sail; but seen from Suderoe, it presented the ap- pearance of a monk, when it received from the Faroese the name of Motiken. The Monk was not merely a picturesque object, it was also a valuable landmark for sailors, warning them against a dangerous whirlpool which swept around its base. But it is now only a thing of the past. Last year a portion of the cliff fell I down, and this year all that remained was broken off just below the waterline, leaving in its place a dangerous reef, which is covered even at low water. Fortunately, it was uninhabited, so no lives were lost. The occur- rence is noteworthy as proving that the continuous wash of the sea, aided probably in the winter by the action of driving ice blocks, is able to saw through immense masses ef rock consisting of hard basalt, cutting them clean across at the water's edge.
PHYSIOLOGICAL APHORISMS. Personal resemblance entails like characteristics of mind and disposition. _ . _

Insanity runs in families ; but, as in the case of family likeness, it sometimes overlaps a generation or more. Inflammations are mere safely and far more agreeably subdued by the 'application of warm water than of cold. Intense thirst is satiated by wading in water, or by keeping the clothing saturat.d with water, even if it 111 taken from the sea.

The foundation of three-fourths of all cases of con- sumption is laid before the age of twenty-five years; in women during their toens. iTo exercise n weariness, increased by every step, is not only not beneficial, it is useless, and worse than useless; it is pOsitively destructive. The hereditary element is not of special account as a cause of consumption, as less than 25 per cent. of CIISCES are clearly of consumptive parentage. One of the ruling causes of disease end premature i death in largo cities s found in an exhausting strain of the mental energies in the struggle for subsistence—a death-race for bread.
No one can possibly sink if the head is thrust entirely under water, and in this position a novice can swim as easily as walk, and to got ashore readily by lifting the head at intervals for breath.

! Very excessive effort in a short space of time, as in running or jumping a rope, &c., has repeatedly caused instant death, by apoplexy of the lungs, the exercise sending the blood there faster than it can be purified by the more infrequent breathing on such occasions. A growing inability to sleep in sickness is ominous of a fatal result; in apparent health, it indicates the failure of the mind and madness; so, on the other hand, in dis- ease or dementia, a very slight improvement in the sleep- ing should be hailed as the harbinger of restoration. No disease ever comes without a warning; hence en- deavour to think back for the cause, with a view to avoid it in future, and on the instant of any unpleasant bodily sensation, cease eating absolutely until it has en- tirely disappeared, at least for 24 hours; if stall remain- ing, consult a physician. The more clothes a man wears, the:more bed-covering he uses, the closer he keeps his chamber, whether warm or cold, the more he confines himself to the house, the more numerous and warm his night-garments:the more readily will he takerpold, under all circumstances, as the more a thriftless youth is helped, the lesspale does-he become be help himself.

As a good tialveller, after having fed his horse, renews his journey not in a trot, but with a slow walk, gradu- ally increasing his pace, so in getting up to address an assembly for a continued effort, the first few sentences should be uttered in a low, slow tone, gradually intensi- fied, otherwise the voice will break down in a very few minutes, with coughing or hoarseness. Water cannot satisfy the thirst which attends cholera, 'dysentery, diarrhcea, and some other forms of disease; ' in fact, drinking cold water seems to increase:the thirst, and induce other disagreeable sensations; but the thirst will be perfectly apd pleasantly subdued by eating a comparatively small amount of ice, swallowing it in as lame pieces as practicable, and as much as is wanted.

LORD BACON AND TRH THAMES FISERRMEN.—The Thames in the olden time was a much cleaner and purer river than at the present day. We read in " Aubrey " that Lord Bacon, being in York House Garden, looking on fishers as they were throwing their nets, asked them what they would take for their draught. They answered so much. His lordship would offer them no More but so much. They drew up their nets, but in it were only two or three little fishes. His lordship then told them that it had been better for them to have taken his offer. They replied they hoped to have taken a better draught; but, said his lordship, 'Hope is a good breakfast, but an ill supper."—" Little Folks" Magazine.

A llonetee Foot—The foot of a horse is One of the I sepst ingenious and unexampled pieces of mechanism in animal structure. The hoof contains a series of vertical and thin lamime of horn, amounting to about 500, and forming a complete lining to it. In this are fitted as many lamitue belonging to the ceffin bone, while both , sets are elastic and adherent. The edge of a quire of paper inserted leaf by leaf into another will convey a sufficient idea of the arrangement. Thus the weight of the animal is supported by as many elastic springs as there are Mime in all the feet, amounting to about 4,000, distributed in the most secure manner, since every spring is acted on in an oblique direction. CLYDESDALE! MASH SOCIETT.—A meeting of the Coun- cil of this society was recently held in Glasgow, Mr. A. Campbell Douglas, of Mains, presiding. Twenty-five new members, including two life governors, were elected. The income for the three months ending Oct. 31st, 1885, was reported to have been £346 155., end the balance at the credit of the society on the same date was £1,394 k. 4d. The second edition of Volume V. was issued on the 4th ult., and Volume VIII. was closed. It will contain over 2,000 entries. A letter from Mr. Wilkie, Christ- church, New Zealand, embodying a proposal to found a benefit society for stallion grooms, was read, and its contents remitted for discussion to a future meeting. Several doubtful pedigrees were discussed and remitted to several members of council for consideration. The pedigree of a horse which was got in Scotland, but foaled in America, was, passed for Volume VIII. The other business was formal. RAPE AND EARLY TURNIPS FOR SARBP.—A very good beginning for sheep that are to be wintered on arable is a piece of rape and white turnips; and nothing beyond the soft white turnip should be left in the ground to be eaten. Aberdeens and gray stones, as well as swedes, had better be cut into finger slices and given in troughs, and there should be a smaller set of troughs for the cake and corn; these last should always be turned bottom upwards when not in use, for if cake is put into a wet trough, or rain falls on it, great waste is occasioned, hence it is better to choose a fine hour for giving the sheep cake. At present prices for mutton, farmers will be cautious how they lay out much money on oilc,ake, though its manurial value must be taken into considera- tion; but to have sheep healthy on turnips we consider oats are essential. It is our practice to let them have some crushed oats the first thing in the morning whilst the first feed of turnips is being prepared. SMALL HoLmmos.—The Earl of Breadalbane, speaking at Stansted, Essex, said that he wished to see the system of small holdings really established in England. He had many on his estates, and the small farmers were the best tenants he had. With the labour required on the larger holdings from those of the lesser ones, they could main- tain a comfortable existence. Every village ought to have a large common. Thousands of acres in this coun- try had been illegally enclosed. He did not wish for the disestablishment of the Church, but was in favour of re- form. The owners of the land and of the tithe ought to be held responsible for the repair of the fabric and for the payment of ministers. In one town in the south of England the tithe was 000, but the clergyman only received £2OO, and no one knew where the rest went to. In an adjoining village no service had been held for two years, because the edifice wanted restoring. This he would remedy by making the owner of the tithe responsible. Fnozast Murroe.—We recently remarked that the price of frozen meat had for some time been so low, averaging less than 4d. per lb. by the carcase, that shippers could scarcely fail to lose money. This expec- tation is confirmed by a report of the proceedings at the last meeting of the Australia Freezing and Export Com- pany, which shows that the business has for some time been carried on at a heavy loss, necessitating a loan of £10,500 at 8 per cent, interest to keep the concern going. To help them out of their difficulties, the Orient Com- pany have agreed to carry frozen meat at the extremely low rate of id. per lb. so long as it does not realise more than 4d. per lb. in,ondon. At first the charge for trans- portation was 2id. per lb., next 2d., and later on 1-id. The very low price now charged cannot pay the Orient Company, who, however, are willing to make a sacrifice rather than have the business discontinued. After the end of this year the squatters are to do their own ex- porting, the Freezing Company restricting its business to freezing the meat. It is said that 100,000 carcases of frozen mutton which arrived in London last July are still on hand and unsold. PULPED POTATOES FOR MILCH Cows.-11aw: potatoes are not good food for mulch cows at this season, as they contain a large amount of acrid acid, which :would be likely to Cause abortion from the way this acrid acid would excite the urinal organs. As an example if potatoes be boiled for pigs, and the water in which they have been boiled is mixed up with the potatoes, the pigs will be purged, unless a large portion of bean meal he mixed with the potatoes and the water in which they were boiled. This acrid acid would at the same time have so great an effect on the milk of cows that it would be difficult as a rule, and probably at times impossible, to get cream to csagulate in the form of butter. If, however, the potatoes be boiled and the water drained away, then they would make excellent food for cows in milk, as they contain much pure starch.—V. A. L.-1 have used pulped potatoes for mulch cows, but do not set much value on them; in fact. I have found steamed potatoes preferable when mashed and mixed with chaff and such kind of short food, especially with the addi- tion of 41b. or 51b, of bean or pea meal and 21b. or 31b. of bran served out daily, and given to each cow in two feeds, morning and evening. Raw potatoes, weight for weight, I do not consider so good as carrots, and cer- tainly they are not as cheap., It would be advisable to sell the potatoes and buy carrots with the money.— Amateur, Surrey.

DOGS AND PARASITFIS.—Everyone has heard of the gid in sheep, known in different parts of the country as the "sturdy." " vertigo," "stagers," " turnside,' or the "whirls." Well, if the brain of an animal that has died of this disease be opened, there will be found therein what are called hydatids or cysts, little bladder-shaped objects. , These are nothing more or less than small colonies of the larvfe of the very large tapeworm, called the To•nia ecenurus. We have scan this parasite nearly two yards long, and repeatedly over one,yard. Each gid hydatid is loaded, so to speak, with hundreds of tape- worm heads, growing from a common centre, and every head, if introduced into the dog's body, is capable of being developed into a tapeworm. The dog often be- comes infested with this parasite from eating sheeps' brains; and dogs thus affficted and allowed to roam at pleasure over fields and hills where sheep are fed, sow the seeds of gid in our flocks to any extent. We know too well the great use of Collie dogs to the shepherd or grazier, to advise that dogs should not be'employed as assistants, but surely it would be to their owner's ad- vantage to see that they were kept in a state of health and cleanliness. Says Cobbold : " Thepropagation of i entozoa in general; and of tapeworms n particular, is intimately connected with, and absolutely dependent upon, the promiscuous association of different kinds of animals; and as regards the production of parasitism amongst domesticated animals used as food, it is per- feetly certain that the tapeworms of the dog play a mos, conspicuous part." Striking language this from so grea, an authority, and affording much food for thought. One of the commonest tapeworms of the dog is the Ttenia marginata. It grows to an immense length. The dog becomes infested from the sheep. The Tcenia echino- coccus is another, very destructive to animal life in the larval state. The Teenia serrata is the tapeworm most commonly found in our sporting dogs. The larva of this entozoon is found in the intestines of the rabbit and hare.--" Book of the Dog" far December. TUE EFFECT OF RENNET ON CIIENSEMAICING.—In the course of a lecture by Mr. J. B. Harris in connection with the Scottish Dairy Association, the speaker said : "Rennet seems to be the only sure agent by which the cheesy matter of milk can be separated from the whey Nature seems to have provided it for the cheesemakers' especial use. Its office is not simply to produce coagu- lation • it goes further, and exercises an important part, not only in the curing of the cheese, but also in bring- ing about that condition which we call digestibility. No other substance of which we have any knowledge is capable of bringing about the same result. In view Of these facts, more than one idea should govern us in the , use of the rennet. If it is intended that the cheese shall go into market in from 40 to 50 days (which should always be the case in the early part of the season with fodder-made cheese) enough of rennet should be used to ensure the process of coagulation beginning in from ten to twelve minutes with milk in proper condition. Ren- net sufficient to accomplish this result will, in the time limited for sale, have performed all that is desired in preparing the product for the table. It will be seen by this, if we have been clear in explaining the idea, that the time of curing rather than the condition and quality of milk should govern the quantity used. Milk, Well matured; will coagulate with less rennet than when sweet and new, but this should make no difference with the quantity used, as the curing of the cheese is what we must consider. If the milk is partly skimmed, or in a,time of year that it is not so rich, more rennet should be used, as the richer the milk the less rennet is re- quired. This is where many cheesemakers fail, who ' never change their quantity in spring, summer, or autumn.. I found many dairies the past season in which splendid cheese was made through June, July, and part of August; but when milk became richer, by reason of the cows giving a less quantity, ' their cheese was soft. If they had decreased their rennet, and increased their heat and salt, their product would have been firm, solid, and good in texture.'

Fritermo Futirr Meas.—This important operation I will for the next two or three months engage the atten- tion of the owners of all gardens that contain fruit teem of any description. Pruning is to cut ofT skilfully super- fluous shoots, in ordor to preserve the symmetry of the tree, regulate the circulation of sap, or to reduce the number of shoots so as to admit more sun and air to those left. All are calculated to ultimately increase the fertility of the tree. The simple act of reducing the ' length of a branch will have the effect of causing numerous fruit buds to form on the portion left. The topmost shoots on young trees are usually more vigorous ' than those lower down, owing to tho greater flow of sap ,1 to those parts, and if we only shorten them the flow of sap is changed in that direction, and a greater flow is I directed to the parts left. Immature wood on fruit trees cannot produce fruit; it is not even capable of resisting the cold of average winters, and it is not improbable that in some instances canker is the result of ruptured, over- charged sap vessels during frost, hence the importance of reducing the number of shoots, so as to expose the re- , mainder to the influence of sun and air. The pruning requirements of the raspberry are, perhaps, the most simple, and amount to merely cutting away all the shoots that bore fruit the previous summer, and reducing the length of those intended to fruit next season, as well as reducing their number to five or seven on each "stool." The Black Currant requires the wood thinned, including some of the thick branches, which should be moved first if they are too thick or have grown naked. All the suckers are also moved, unless any are required to be trained to fill up gaps. As a rule, the young shoots are left their full length, though some growers make a Pm' I tice of shortening them one-fourth. Other varieties of currants require little more pruning than shortening all young growth (excepting the leader) to within four or six eyed from their starting point. The leader is left a ; few inches longer, and all suckers are entirely moved, ' unless there is a probability of any of the main branches ; decaying, then a young one should be selected te fill up ' the gap. Gooseberries, on the other hand, require prun- ing similar to the Black Currant, and tone of the shoots should ho nearer than 6in. to each ether. Many growers shorten the young wood to about half-a-dozen eyes, but we prefer leaving them their entire length, except where they unduly extend so as to destroy the symmetry of the tree, and:alL inferior and unnecessary shoots are cut close to the old wood. The practice of shortening back all the shoots:as above has a tendency to create a perfect thicket of wood, that increases the labour of pruning, whereas if the shoot is reduced to an eye or two the number of now shoots will be one-sixth less. Tea Faoarr GARDIM—Many of the herbaceous plants that are cut down would be benefited if covered over with fine ashes to the depth of 3in. or 4in. Some of the Pensternons might be saved in this way; Tritorna Uvaria (or the Red-hot Poker Flower) might have some packed round its crowns for protection from frost; Delphiniums, Phloxes, and Hollyhocks require it more for protection from the ravages of slugs, which are always on the look- out for the young shoots as soon as they begin to push early in the spring. Pansies. Violas, Polyanthus, Auricu- las, and plants of such like growth might he defended from these pests if girdled round with ashes, as the snails dislike travellinif over this material. 'Prm VRNDOW.—The Fern Case: The occupants of this will not require the amount of water at the root they have hitherto, and none must be given overhead; and if there are any traces of decay on the fronds, more air must be admitted to dispel the damp. It has been pointed out in this column that the fern case is the best medium for raising seedling ferns. The forerunner of the young ferns is a kind of moss not unlike the lime- worts, so that any Mossy vegetation should be left un- disturbed. The spores of most of the ferns vegetate from three to six months after they are distributed. The best time to pot these young seedlings is from May to the end of July, as the warmth will encourage rapid root formation.

Roberts, in his address to the Senate on resigning the office of Senior Proctor, makes the following remarks :—" It has been my lot to hold the office of proctor a second time, after an interval of some years. It is inevitable that this circumstance should suggest some sort of a comparison. / do not wish to deceive myself with any illusory notions that all beneath the surface is as perfect as we know it is ,not, and as we do not despair that it may be. But I desire to put it on record, as a matter of common ob- servation, and I do so without fear of contradiction, that, during the interval covered by the past eight years, the gain to order' decency, and morality, in every:sense of the word, has been immense." It is significant that this period of eight years, which Mr. Roberts's experience i covers, is that n which the medical school has grown from comparative insignificance to its present strength and influence. His testimony is corroborated by many, experienced college tutors, and effectually dispels the forebodings of some who saw in an increased efflux of medical students to the University a source of danger to tone and bearing, and morality. It is admitted now that hard-working purposeful medical student has added a needful element of steadiness and energy to the body of undergraduates.—British Medical Journal. WEAN AND TXAR OF GOLD.—The annual loss of gold, by attrition, shipwreck, fires, &c., is very small, not quite two tons, or £280,000. According to Jevons, gold win loses 2 per cent. in 100 years—that IS, £147,000 per annum on the actual amount, £736,000,000. The loss by shipwreck cannot possibly be higher than one-sixth of the ratio of loss in sea-borne merchandise—say, £2 for every. £l,OOO shipped; and as the quantity of sea-borne gold m 1871-80 averaged £50,400,000 per annum, the loss by shipwreck would be £lOl,OOO. If we allow £32,000 for loss by fires, we make up a total wear and tear of £280,000, or two tons, the existing stock being a trifle under 11,000 tons. Mc.Culloch used to reckon for jewel- lers, loss, wear and tear, '&c., about per cent, which would be nearly £4,000,000 a year of our present stock. The " consumption " by jewellers is probably even more now, but this nowise affects the question of a possible gold famine, since the jewellers' consumption goes to swell the uncoined reserve. It would appear that 80 years ago the uncoined reserve was better understood than to-day, for I find in the Edinburgh Review of 1803 the following passage :—" The precious metals have a Itwofold use—for manufactures and coin. If there is a deficiency of coin the plate will be melted and coined. If there is a superabundance of coin it will be melted and monufactured.—Contemporary Review. LITXDRIANT AND SILKY HAIR.—Alrs. S. AT MANDALAY. RANGOON,iSuNDAY.—King Thelma, has arrived here. No deoinion has yet been taken as to leis ultimate deetination. The Chamber of Commerce Of this city has addressed a me- modal to Mr. Bernard, Chief Commissioner of British Bar- mah. The Chamber further -expresses its conviction that natives of Upper turnmh by their steady immigration into Lower Burmab tacitly concur in demanding the complete annexation of their country. Lucarrow, SATVEDAY.--Lord Dufferin,hart arrlved here., Replying to an address presented by the municipel authora ties, his Excellency said it was fortunate that the nbject of the expedition to Barmah had been attained without rteriouel loss to either side. The authorities, on the spot had tele- ' graphed that nothing . was more satisfactory than the , friendly spirit of the population, The Viceroy, in'teonclu- sion, deOlared that whatever might be done with 'lndia, it would not Commit the Home Government to any line of action which wotild not ultimately merit the approval of the English peoPle. . . • Mattoaaav, WEDNESDAY.—On the evening of the King's departure there was some dacoiting in Mandalay. A few of the inhabitants were killed by the robbers. Our pickets ;alight six of the deceits, who were formally sentenCed to death. A regular !system of petrel tate been initituteci. The inhabitants are generally resuming their btiehteesdind trade ,is reviving Neven of the Kiog'a half slaters have been re,- I leased hbm prison, after baying suffered six years' oaptivity. They speak bitterly of the Queen's cruel treatmeet, and ex- press unbounded delight at the arrivatof the British. committee has been ranking an appraisement of the King's possessions, and of the money in the treasury. Much ad the Royal property was carded off ;on, the morning of the British occupation, and the estimate of Vane placed by the committee on what was found in the nitwit is thegefore a low one. 4 meeting of the King's Ministers was held yes- terday, when all acquieseed Thetiaw's "dedirenemeoti They appear disposed te be loyal; and are actively assieting the English officials in disarming the native inhabitants. If I. reported that M. Haas, the French consul, sidVd the King to surrender when resistance to the British expedition was found to be useless.. ,An , enormous ,quantity of srme has been given no to tbeßritleb: . MANDALAY, Entnea.-e-freveral Prendergast halt issued another proclamation addressed to all woons and civil and military officers of the Burmese Empire. It states that until the will of the Empress of India be known the civil and military administration rests in the hands of General Prendergast, who desires to carry en the Government with the aid of the Ministers, Governors, and other officers of the State how in office who wish to remain loyal to the British Governmeet. Priests will be allowed to continue their religious duties, and all persons will be unmolested pro- vided that they remain quiet and peaceable. All civil and military officers are invited to return to their ditties on con- dftion. that they undertake to discharge them faithfully. All important matters are to be referred to the civil officer. Every effort will be made to repress crime, and all, vagrante ancirlacolts are ,directed to continue forwarding revenue through the woon to the civil officers. All officials are to Reek orders from the Councis of Ministers at Mandalaya Finally, the proclamation declares that anyone injuring or illtreating a &lash subjeet will be' severely dealt with. The document' bears the signature of General ,Prendergast. The *proclamation has been received by the Burmese with much satisfaction. SERVIA .AND BULGARIA'. - FAIRE OF THE CONFERENCE—RESUMPTION OF WAR EXPECTED.' Ntscn, SArtannar.—The Bulgarian conditions of peace are as follows a—The Servians to evacuate the Widdin dis-1 tract, and the-Bulgarians to evacuate Pirot ; Servia to pay an-Indemnity of 30,000,000 marks, and Bulgaria to retain Firot until the money is paid. The Servians decline to ac- cept the terms, and the war is expected to be renewed. BELGRADE, BATURDAY.—CoIoneI Sava Grnics bait been appbinted Minister at St. Petireburg in the room of General Horvatoviteb. This appointment is regarded as indirating a rapprochement between Servia 'and Russia, Col. Cruica being known for hit Russian sympathies. A report in cur- rent thie,evenieg that Bulgaria_bas offered new nonditione Of peace, the principal stipulation being an offentive and tlefensiye alliance with Servia against Turkey. -CONSTANTINOPLE, SATURDAY.—At the last Meeting of the Ambassedo-s, Herr Von Radcyitz and Said Pasha re- proached Sir W. White with impeding the work of pacify- ing Ronmalia by bie objection to the Sultan's -proclamation to the people of Eastern Ronmelia. Other members of the Conference,•with the exception of the Marquis de Neailles, also disapproved the course adopted by Sir ,William White. The Porte modified the proclamatien three times, but the British Minister nevertheless insisted theta mixed commis- sion should previously be sent te ascertain the wishes of the Roumelian people._ It is believed that the re-establishment of the status quo ante will,be found impossible without bloodshed. Gertnary is using her inflaefficelo bridging about n reconciliation and an understanding between Prince Alexander, the Czar, and the Sultan. BELGRADE, Sum:ay.—Russia and Austria have decided Ito take itnmediate action in the event of a renewal of hosti- lities, the former occupyine Bulgaria and Austria sending troops into Servia. The French Government acquiesces in the propos-d action of the two Empires. The condoned suspension of hostilities is therefore expected. BELGRADE, MONDAY.—The Servian Government received Information from the Porte last night that the Sultan had 'telegraphed to Prince Alexander ordering him to prolong the suspension of hostilities, and declaring that his High- ness had not the right to negctiate. The Net Servian pro- posal to Bulgaria is to continue the armistice for one mbnth both aides maintainiog their present positions. Servia has been advised to remain on the defensive, and to emelt the intervention of the Powers. The suspension of hostilities sill be maintained at least till the 9th inst. It-is not, how- ever, expected that Bulgaria will be satisfied without some "bbticession on the part of Servia,-and the despatch of troops to the front is therefore proceeding. Arms also continue to arrive from abroad. SOFIA. TUESDAY—The Bulgarian Government last night presented a note to the representatives of the Powers de- claring its inability to depart from the terms first offered to Benda. The Government further declares, so far as re- garde the restoration of peace, that it will continue to evince tta same modest disposition as in the past, feeling sure the Powers will take the Bulgarian victories and sacrifices into account. The Bulgarian Government, in replyieg to-day to Servian counter proposils, notified its adherence to its first proposals for an armistice, and entree &reic accepts them within 24 hours declares its in'ention of referring to the Powers, through whose intervention the Bulgarians dis- continued hostilities. PRINCE ALEXANDER CONGRATULATED. PRILIPPOPOLIS, 'WEDNESDAY. Different deputations from the provinces before leaving here held a meeting yes- terday evening, at which a committee was elected, charged to assist the Government to attain the complete union of Bulgaria and Eastern Reumelia A telegram was dcspatcbed to Prince Alexander informing His Highnedit of tbe appoint- ment of the Committee, and congratulating him upon the victories be had achieved. The excitement of the inhabi- tants has in a great measure -subsided. There are now over 15000 recruits in this city. • - NISH, WEDNESDAY.—The reply of Prince Alexander re- fusing the Servian counter proposals was received' here last night.- 'The Prince begs King Milan to declare within 24 hours if he now accepts the Bulgarian-conditions previously proposed, namely, that the Servisos -should evacuate Bul- garian. territory, after which the Bulgarians will' evacuate Servian territory on receiving assurance of the conclusion of pence. Gmeral Horvatovica is constantly engaged in inspecting Servian positions, and planting extensions of entrenchments. Toe strength of the Nisbava army now exceeds 100,000 men. The troops are well supplied with ammuni- tion. •

BELGRADE, THURSDAY.—The Ssrvian Government last night sent a circular to all foreign Ministers here, informing them that they cannot accept the Bulgarian conditions, be- cause they are dishonourable, and that hottilities will therefore be resumed this evening. The Government adds, however, that the army will cease hostilities should the Powers be able to arrange an honourable peace. The cir- cular is signed by M. Garaschanine. A meeting of the foreign representatives will be held immediately. German influence here continues to be exercised strongly in favour of peace. SPAIN.—GENERAL PARDON FOR POLITICAL OFFENCES. MADRID, TUESDAY. A Cabinet Council last night de- cided upon the terms of a decree granting a general pardon ter all politica and press offence.. It is understood that the pardon will include all political exiles except military officers guilty of rebellion when actually holding command. Toe latter, however, may solicit the Royal clemency, and th,,ir cases will be considered separatdy. All existing press prosecutions are to be abandoned, and all journalists now in prison will be releas,d. MADRID, THDRSDAT,—The official gazette this morning publishes a R iyal decree, signe•l by the Queen Regent, granting a general pardon to all prisoners and political offenders, excepting those persons who are subjected to mili.ary laws, and who have committed offences against military EGYPT AND THE SOCDAN.—RENEWED FIGHTING. _ATTACK, ON THE BRITISH GARRISON.

_ WADI HALFA, SATURDAY.—The post at Ambigol Wells having been again attacked, a fore's under General Butler from Akasheh advanced at dayiight this morning from the break in the railway south of the post, while Colonel Huy- elle, with four companies of the Berkshire Regiment, ad- ' "need simultaneously from the north. The relsels with- drew from their Position and communication with Ambigoi a•;0.19 has been re-eataibed. The post has been strongly reinforced, and the railway is being repaired. The enemy are in fe.irci: at Kosheb, ht seem disinclined to attack, aod! I are beginning, to entrench. CAIRO, FRIDAY —Post at Ambigol Wells attacked by the enemy with one gun besides amall.arms. After some hours' fitihting enemy beaten off and retired south. Casualties : Killed, one Berkshire ; wounded slightly, one Royal FA- eiei ll HL,E nnteeTru rl e oss,s repotted. I engaged the ad- vance party of 1,000 men with Gardner and rifisa with con- siderable effect. Several men carrying banners, three hems- men, and a number of footmen rolled over. Gun fired one round at Lotus, but shot fell short. Gardner very well

At Kosheh the enemy have settled down and made a work for their guns. Numerous deserters come in. The blacks. thelr best troops, seem to be leaving them. Three hundred deserted yesterday in a body, and went south by

_ the west bank. CAIRO, MONDAY.—General Stephenson has been ordered to the South on accpunt of the supposed critical position of affairs there. He will leave on Saturday. Four thousand Arabs are intrenchad two miles south Of Ikasha. The re- cent action of Italy at Massowah took the Egyptian autho- rities by surprise. The Italian Consul-General here was asked for explanations on the subject, but replied that be had no information. The Khedive thererpon sent a tele- gram to the sultan. It is believed that the Turkish Ambas- sador at Rome will be instructed to request explanations from the Italian Government. After the arrival of Sir Henry Drummond Wolff the Italian:Government complained of difficulties being caused by the Egyptian Administration at Massowah and demanded the transfer of the civil , administration to the Italian authorities. The Egyp- tian Government, however, refused its assent, and this re- ply met at the time with the approval of the British,Go- vernment. TURCOMAN DEMAND FOR RUSSIAN PROTECTION. VIENNA, MONDAI.—The Russian papers state that Tur- cornan and Usheg envoys from Northern Afghanistan have arrived at Mery to implore Russian protection against Afghan cruelties. Prince Dondottkoff Sorsakoff imme- diately left for Askabad, and the Russian occupation of the Turcomon territory is shortly expected. FRANCE.—THE TAXATION OF IMPORTED FOOD. PARIS. MONDAY.-1 he Chamber to-day, by 338 yvtes against. 174, decided to take into consideration the proposals demanding an increaee in the duty on cereals and cattle. The Minister of Agriculture, while offering no opposition to the decision, asked the Chamber whether, after the recent increase of duty, a further augmentation was advisable with- out first waiting the effect of the previous increase. The Minister pointed out that although recent years had been favourable to French' agriculture, a less satisfactory period was tube apprehended, for which reason. foreign products should not be excluded from French markets. PRINCE BISMARCK'S ArnruDE.

PAnts..Txuasnay.--It is reported here on trustworthy authority that Piince Bismarck has made a Strong repro- sentatien te Austria awl Russia on the necessity for main- tenance of .the peace of Europe. Lie is reported to have said in the hearing of a well-known diplomatist that he would not allow an.ther to disturb the old age of the Em- peror William if he could possibly help it. Daring the last few days he has accordingly intervened in thQ Servis- Bulgarian difficulty with a view to bringing the rupture be an end.

TIIF. NATIOstAt Liberal Club on Wednesday resolved t! establish a " Wters' Protection Society." for the purpose of taking nu cases of intimidation and other breaches of the Corrupt Practices Act and, where found desirable. carrying them into court. It was stated that several cases bad already been reported to the committee. CHURCH DEFENCE.—A Church defence meeting was held on Wednesday in Manchester tinder the presidency of Lord Egerton of Tattoo. The Chairman said in face of the pre- sent condition of things it was ne-dful for Churchmen, whether Liberal or Conservative, to combine in cpposition to the common eneny for maintaining the union of Church and State, and he hoped to see a league formed with that end in view. WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE SOCIETY —The annual meeting of the Manchester National Society for Women's Suffrage was held at the Manchester Town Hall on Wednesday, under the presidency of the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Gold- schmidt). In the 'report it was stated that the position of the movement was very encouraging. and that the commit- tee bad confident hooes of the settlement of the question at an early date in the history of the new Parliament. A large majmity of the members for England and Wale had ex- pressed tl-1 meelves in favour of the principle which the society advocated. The report having been adopted, a resolution was passed, on the motion of Dr. Watts, seconded by Miss Becker, requesting Mr. Woodall, M.P., to take the earliest opportunity possible of introducing a bill for the extension of the Parliamentary franchise to women. A resolution appointing the Executive Committee for the year gave rise to a warm debate. In the first list proposed the flaw of Miss Becker, the secretary, who has served con- tinuously on the committee for eighteen years, was omitted. Mr. Alderman Bennett nroposed some additional names. including that of Wei Becker. The R4v. S. A. Steinthal (treasnrer), Mr. J. P. Thomason, Mrs. Srcatcherd, and others, objected to Miss Becker being again placed on tile committee, as they had, through various reasons, found it impossible to work with her. By a majority of 54 to 21 the meeting adopted the motion of Mr. Alderman Bennett. The Mayor expressed a hoot that some modus vivendi would be. fonnd, but Mr. Steinthal declared, for himself and other workers of The committee, that the only way they saw out of the difficulty, after the decision of the meet- ing, was to resign. • •• MT SWEILTH,ART!..—MiS9 Minnie Palmer is as swat; r favourite here as in America.
