THE GENERAL ELECTION- INCIDENTS AND HUMOURS. Deseronexce AT FARNBOROUOIL—During the polling in the Northern Division of Soinersetehire on Tuesday some serious rioting occurred. At Farnborough e gun was twice tired through the window of a polling ttotiou, but no oae was injured. Many windows were broken by stone throw- ing, and numerous arrests were made. Special constables were employed to quell the disturbance, and several troops et yeomanry were called out. AcrioN FOR LIBEL.—Dr. Pankhuret has commenced an action against Colonel C. E. liatnilton, M.P. for Rother- hither, in respect of a statement circulated prior to the election, charging him with being an Atheist, and hav- ing made use of the following expreseion in the Town Hall, Manchester—"lf there be a God, I defy him ; and if there be a Devil, I am in a position to defy him too." Dr. Pankhurat is of opinion that this charge had much to do with his defeat. FATAL RESULT OF AN ELECTION DISTURBANCE.—At Shef- fir Id. on Monday, an inquest was held on the body of Mr. Horocastle, a druggist, and the evidence showed that the deceased, who was 68 years of age, was standing near the doorway at a meeting held during the election by the sup- porters of Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, when an attempt was maite to eject a person who bad interrupted the proceedings, and in the rush the deceased was thrown down some steps. Hie thigh was fractured, and a day or two ago be died from the shock to the system. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." SERIOUS ACCIDENT.—During a procession in Ealing, on Saturday atone:MO, in honour of Lord G. Hamiltoe, two serious accidents occurred. Colonel Prendergast Walab, of Ealing, fell out of a waggonette whilst standing up to bow to Lady G. Hamilton, and sustained severe injuries to his head. Afterwards, in Uxbridge-road, a pony attached to a baker's cart, trightened by a horn blown in the proces- sion, ran away, and Mr. leash, of Ealing, a member of firm of London solicitors, trying to stop it, was knocked down, and a wheel of the cart passed over his body. He was badly bruised, and suffered much from the shock, but no boner were broken. "Sown. COMMONS ”—" Ecroydism " end "Fair Trade" have been the subjects of many witticisms. One tale which is going the round of North-East Lancashire may be con- sidered worth repeatiug. It is reported that after the Roseendale election, one of the farmers in this district, who was fattening his pigs ready far killieg, took them only two bells of meal instead of three, as was customary.- It is stetA that one of the pigs, being left without its usual supply, suddenly, like Baalem's ASS, became gifted with the power of speech. Looking up to its owner with an injured e epee-talon' it is reported to have said, "What! has Ecroyd got in? Is there a tax put on food that I have te go on short Commons? " A VICAR'S WIFE ON MR. CiLABSTONS.—A Chester cor- respondent writes —"A: vicir's wife in Flintshire, who has been canvassing the working-men for Mr. Moetth against Lord Richard Grosvenor, is excessively angry, because she declares that, while they all pledged theme-Ives to vote for Mr. Mostyn, as a matter of fact they all plumped for Lord R. Grosvenor. The usual Christmas charities are in course of distribution, end the vicar's wife is angrily threatening- that if she could diecever who had played her such a trick she would stop the doles. She added that in her opiaion. Mr. Gledstone was demented altogether when he passed an Act of Parliament giving such men the vote. 'i hey were utterly unworthy of such a sacred trust after her experience of their conduct" ROZOIIS AT PONTEFEACT.—At Featherstone, near Fonts, tract, on Friday eight, Mr. George Senior, manager at the Featherstone Manor Colliery, was set upon by the roughs ' because he did not show yellow favours, and was kicked , unmercifully and his shoulder bens broken. The Junction Hotel was attacked mei 104 panes of glass broken. The Sta- tins hotel was also assailed and damage done to the extent of 'about £4O. The shops of Messrs. Cowling, Hemingway, , Maxwell, and the Conservative Club were all fired at by the molt with stones end great damage dons. Mr. Hirst, a t farmer, and Mr. Maxwell, a shopkeeper, brought out fire- alms to protect themselves and their property, and fired to I deter the roughs. Damage to the extent of hundreds of pounds has been done, BALL AT CLITHEROE LIBERAL CLEI3.—On Tuesday even- ing a d ince, promoted by the members, was held in the large room of the Liberal Club, Clitheroe, in honour of Sir Ughtred Kav-Sbuttleworth'e magnificent victory. There , was a large attendance. The ticket otadmission was headed ; with the figures 2,359, being the majority by which Sir Ughtred was returned as first member for the Clitheroe Division. The room was suitably embellished for the in. teresting event. Appropriate mottoes adorned the walls, , amongst which shone conspictioesly " Success to our New ' .Member," " Hurrah for Sir Ughtred and his tnagnificent t majority, 2,359,y " Unity is strength ; both sides of Pendle ; Hill are now united ; long may it last," and " Long life to , ; the Midlothian hero" In commemoration of the victory there was a display of fireworks at the Liberal Club on Saturday evening. SIR WILFRED Lawsox.—lt is remarkable to find that Sir W. Lawson, the leader of the Temperance Party in the last Parliament, was defeated by a Conservative teetotaller—Mr. Valentine. Sir Wilfred's absence from the House causes a "void not easily filled. If there was one man more than another who could keep the House in good humour that t man TM Sir Wilfrid Lawson. Extremely witty and quick at repartee, be had that rare faculty of giving home thrusts to his opponents without creating a bitter personal feeling. , His jokes were always original, and always to the point. It is probable, however, that he will not greatly regret his ex- clusion from the House of Commons. He has been in ill- health for some time, and greatly needs rest. In his retire- ment he will be able calmly to watch the course of events in the House, and to recruit his strength for a future battle tl which cannot be far off. Mo. CHILDERS.—The defeat of Mr. Childers at Ponte- , tract was a severe blow to the Liberal party, but it cannot be said to have been unexpected. It was Mr. Childers who introduced the Budget which led to the downfall of the Liberal party in the House of Commons, and gave op- portunity for Sir M. Hicks-Beach to intimate his desire of increasing the tax on tea in preference to touching the liquor-interest. Mr. Childers' financial proposals as Cban- cellor of the Exchequer made him specially obnoxious to the supporters of Beer and the Bible, who, if the cry of " The Church in Danger" fails, can always rally their supporters round the banner of "The poor man's beer." Both these factors played an imp ,thant part in the defeat of Mr. Childers. The country is not likely, however, to lose the valuable services of the right hon. gentleman. It is re- ported in Frome that Mr. Lawrence Baker will retire from the representation of that division to enable Mr. Childers to regain a seat. in Parliament. LORD CRANBORNE AT lIITFIRLD.—Visconnt Cranhorne received a hearty welcome home at Hatfield on his return from Damen, the townspeople taking the opportunity of expressing their satisfaction, in a very demonstrative faith- ion, at the successful issue of the contest fought by his lordship in Lthcashire. A plentiful display of bunting, and a capital triumphal arch, imparted a festive appearance to Hatfield town. On emerging from the station loud cheers greeted him, the horses were taken from the est-Hags sent to meet him, a body of working men took their places, and a procession beaded by a band, and comprising members of Conservative Associations and the Primmee League, escor- ted him to Lord Salisbury's mansion. There an address of cnneratulation orr his election as a member of Parlia- ment was presented, and elicited a brief reply of thanks. Refreshments were supplied to those who chose to partake of them, and in be evening a torchlight procession conducted the Viscount through the illuminated streets of the town to afield, where a large bonfire was lighted. THE CAUSE OF LIBERAL REVERSES --Mr. Arthur Arnold, Salford, Writ,`ll to the Times as follows :—" The opinion ex- pressed by one of your correspondents that the greatest contest is not between Liberals and Coneervatives, but be- tween Liberals and Radicals,' appears ridiculous to one who has had experience such as mine. I keow my late conetitu• ency very intimately. I do not know tent single Liberal vote which was lost to our cause in the recent election. The union of Liberals and Eidicald was complete. My candida- ture was honoured with the personal advocacy on the plat- form of the Dean of Manchester, Sir Henry James, and Mr. Jacob Bright, together with every prominent Liberal and Radical in the division nf North Salford. Our organisation wee so efficient that we polled 44 per cent of the whole con- stituency. I had all the advantage of an opponeet who•de- scribed himself es 'a Tory of the old school,' and his policy as' net alteration of the Land Laws.' Why, then, was I beaten? My story is that of other candidates. Solely by order of Mr. Parnell, who controlled perhaps 400 or 500 votes." MR. W. E. BRIGGS —The defeat of Mr. Briggs at Black- burn is keenly felt by the Liberals of that town ; but he himself is looking forward, with good heart, to the turn of the wheel During the late contest he addressed many Liberal .meetings in various parts of the country. At one of these places a man at the back of the hall continually in- terrupted the meeting by calling out, "Speak up!" and then, when the hon. gentleman had pitched his voice in a higher key, he shouted " Louder !" Being unable to con- tinue his speech in the face of these repeated interruptions, Mr. Briegs said—" I will tell my friend at the rear of the hall a story; and, as it will not rebate to this political con- troversy, perhaps he will hear rue. A senator in Cincinnati was addressing a large gathering one day, when a man kept calling out, 'Speak louder! louder!' Tne senator. becom- ing at last rather angry, said, Look here, friends ; I believe when the archangel Gabriel Founds the last trump, some foil In Cincinnati will yell `Lou:ler ! louder ! " Tee audience fairly shouted with delight, and for the remainder of the meeting Mr. Beiges was permitted to continue his remarks without interruption. Rummies OF Hoooorts.—The honours and rumours of honours from the Tory Premier point to an expectation of an early Termination of office. " Atlas," in the World, cets:—" It is rumoured that the Duke of Norfolk has de- client the Garter, and that it will be given to Lord Carnet- von. Sir Massey Lopes, whose eon was last week beaten in south Devon, where no Liberal has been successful since Lord John Russell was turned out, just 50 years ago, is to be raised to the peerage. His father, the late Sir Manassah lopes, was made a baronet as a reward for having vacated his seat for Westbury in 1t29 to make room for Sir Robert Peel, after that statesman had been rejected by the Uniyer- eity of Oxford. Sir Matthew White Ridley is also to 13e r iised to the peerage. lle is the head of one of the oldest and richest families in Northumberland, and his predeces- ., 'es at Blegdon could 3t any time have obtained a peerage -tom Mr. Pitt or Lord Liverpool. George 111. was very par- ial to the Rid', y family, because he connected them in some cloudy way with the bishop who was burnt at Oxford by Bloody Mary," and they were closely related to his pet, Lord Eldon. Sir Watkio Williams Wynn is to be offered an earldom, a distinction which was refused by his grandfather

from Lord Liverpool, and by his groat-grandfather from Mr. Pitt", st "'• • TOOTING AT WEDICOME—The polling dieWtt of Wed- more, for the Wells Division of Somersetsleiro, was the scene Ma tetrible riot on the day of the election, which re- milted in favour of Colonel Phget, Conservative candid:ate. On Friday the disturbance commenced by some Radicals waling, from the house of a prominent Conservative a blue flag. The Conservatives went after the flag, and a fight eneued, the Radicals taking refuge in a public-house. The few police in the neigbbouritood did their beet to dieperee the mob; but with little effect, the rioters pelting them with stones, which cut some of the constables about the face. Later in the day the riot was renewede acd a public- house ' whicn was wrecked during the afternoon was again attacked. The mob broke open the house, and severely handled those within, but were beaten off. Those outside again pelted the Radicals in the house, and the latter retaliated by the use of firearms. There were pointed at the-mile through broken windows, and• discharged again and again for fully two hours, several persons being struck by shots. One man lies in a critical condition, the bullets entering his abdomen and thigh, whilst another man was dangerously wounded in the leg. Matters became so serious that extra police were tele- graphed for, but in the meantime the mob marched to the police statiou, which they attacked with sticks and stones, breaking every window, as well as sashes. RUROVRED TORY PROGRAIIIIR.—A statement has been circulated which professes to contain the legislative projects of her Majesty's Ministers for the eneuipg session. It is said that the Government will introduce a bill to amend the Education Act of 1870 by providing, under less onerous conditions than at present, for the payment of school fees on behalf of parents too poor to pay them for themselves. County Government Bill, it is further announced, will be brought in, and its provisions extended to Ireland. Radical changes, we are told, will be introduced into the administra- tion of Ireland from Dublin Castle, and a more popular system sobstituted.. The Lord Chancellor is to introduce a bill for facilitating the transfer of land, for establishing registration courts, and for enabling the Ecclesiasticel Commissioners to sell their land. There is to be a new Shipping Bill, and a new Electric Lighting Bill, while as for Home Rule the Governmest will wait to hear what Mr. Parnell eays. There is nothing new and nothing authori- tive in 'hese Resertions. Most of them are taken from what may he celled the Newport programme, in which Lord Salisbery borrowed so largely from Mr. Gladstone's mani- trete.. Lord Randolph Churchill has publicly advocated the sort of mekeseift semi-free Education Bill here refer- red to. At the Municipal Corporations dinner in October Mr. Arthur Balfour remarked that a County Government Bill would have to be introduced, whatever Government was in power. MOONLIGHT OUTRAGE BY TORIES —OR the night of the 2nd met, a malicious outraee was constnitted on the house of the Rev. G. C. Cetterell,llaptist minister, of Borough- bridge, by some person or persons connected with the Tory party. Some time between twelve and six o'clock on the morning of the 3rd inst, the lower front windows of his house, with door and porch, which stand conspicuous in the highway leading to Ripon, were thickly covered with dark blue paint, 23 broad crosses being drawn on the win- dows, and the door smeared with paint from top to bottom, while the large doors of entrance to the coachhoese and gardon were painted in large blue letters "Vote for Daw- nay," and each post with a cross stretching most of the way down. Mr. Catterell, who resides on the north side of ~th 3 river and in the Thirsk and Malton Division, is a pro flounced Liberal, but has taken little active part in the elec- tion beyond writing a letter which appeared in the York Herald of the 27th November, giving a truthful report of the action of the Tory party in Boroughbridee and the neighbourisocol, and passing a fair and temperate criticism upon Toryism in general. But the sting of the letter lay in its truth; and the leaders of the party t)ok alarm at it, and for days their bitterness knew no bounds. On the night of the declaration of the poll for the Ripon Division, when they found themselves defeated, some of the more ex- citable of the party were heard to vow vengeance on the writer of the letter, timely warnieg of which was given to Mr. Catterell through the police ; bat on the same night their malice found vent in this outrage on his house. SCRUTINIES PEIIANDED.—One of the most striking fea- tures of the election is the number of scrutinies which have bele demanded. Already four are announced, namely, in the Ashton-under-Lyue Division of Lancashire, Cocker- mouth (Cumberland), Appleby (Westmorland), and High Peak (Derbyshire). In each constituency the Conservative candidate has been declared euceeesful, and in each inatance the primary groiind on which scrutiny is demanded is the narrow majority by which the Liberal candidate was defeated. At High Peak Mr. J. F. Cheetbam was defeated by a majority of nine ; at Appleby Alderman Whitehead was defeated by a majority of ten ; at Cockermouth Sir W. Lawson had to yield through tha same majority; and Mr. Hugh Mason was diricarded by Ashton-uoder-Lyne Division by a majority of 46. The proposal to have a scrutiny of the votes polled in the Darwen Division election is still under consideretioe, by the committee of investigation rip• pointed by the Liberals, and is not yet settled upon. It is , true that suliscriptions have been solicited, and already labout £l.OOO has been subscribed for the purpose; but the , heads of the Liberal party are disinclined to put the town to the expense of a protracted and contested scrutiny. The return shown the number of votes polled for Viscount Cran- borne to have been 5,878, and for Mr. J. G. Potter 5,873. As the number of registered electors is 12,269, this leaves only 513 electors unpolled. It is further said that there are grounds for calculating that, even in so short a time as has elapsed since the registration, either through3l ee•s or death, 6 per cent, must be deducted as incapable) r This would give 736. If this conclusion is correct, n ,e must have been 218 personatiens of electors dead or int it in bed. Again, to the above must be added those who through removal had become unknown, or who, from being non-resi- dent or otherwise, were unable to come to the poll. MR. PARNELL AND TER CRISIS.-10 an interview with a correspondent of the Boston Herald on Saturday night, Mr. Parnell said that if the Nationalist candidate were suc- cessful in South Tyrone, the Irish party would consist of 86 members. The Irish Tories would be represented by 18 members, while the Irish Liberals would be without a single seat. He stated that large remittances had been received from America to defray Nationalist election expenses, but further subscriptions were more pressing than ever, because R coesiderable number of the new members would require financial help to enable them to maintain a constant attend- ance in Parliament. Mr. Parnell added—" These electien results in the hands of the English leader who may propose a Constitution for Ireland can be used with enormous effect es showing the overwhelming preponderance of the Nationalist party in Ireland, and the utter insignificance of the minority, to the defence of whose unjust privileges the forces of the Empire have been directed for so many cen- turies. At this moment it is very difficult to predict whether the Liberals will have a majority over Tories and Nationalists combined, or whether the Tories and National- ists combined will have a majority over the Liberals. But it looks as if the majority on either side would not exceed ten. Therefore it seems to me that the next Parliament cannot last long. In the new Parliament our policy must be guided by circumstances. We cannot say what it will he till we have beard the declaration of the English party leaders on the Irish question. One thing, however, is cer- tain, the Irish question will be the question unless foreign complications arise. Ido not believe in the possibility of a coalition Government. I see no converging lines between any considerable section of the two English parties; but even if such a combination were possible, it would not, as experience shows, last long. Coalition Ministries in Eng- land have always been short-lived. I doubt whether the Conservatives could detach as many as twelve men from the Liberal ranks for the purpose of a coalition, and even if they could the dozen or so detached would be a very poor substitute for our 86 votes. I expect the settlemeet of the Irish question to come from the Liberals. Assuming that they will be about equal to the Tories and Nationalists corn- bineNit would be in our power, oh their acceptance of our terms, to dire them at once a majority of 170 votes, which, even making allowance for considerable defections from their own ranks, would be Amply sufficient to enable them to deal with the Irish qaestion and every ether ques- tion; whereas the Conservatives cannot, even with our aid, get more than a bare majority, and would be always hampered by the action of their 18 or 19 followers from reland."

The discovery has caned some sensation. • THE UNITe D STATES.—NOMINATION OF VICE- PIiffiSIDENT. NEW Yonx, SATURDAY.—Mr. Btiertaitin has been nomi- nated as President of the Senate.' The nominationis eqeiva- lent to election. The President of the Senate becomes ex- officio Vic• President of the Republic, and by the election of Mr. Sherman provision is made for filling the Presithney in case of the disability of Mr. Cleveland. The Democrats have nominated Mr. Carlisle as Speaker of the ,House of Representatives. The nomination is equivalent to election.• . THE PRESIDENT'S MEsSAGE. WASHINGTON, TUESDAY —The Prf:Bilifqll.2B Me1,q4211 11.1.1 ' been transmitted to Congress to-day. :It commences by re- ferring in feeling terms to the death of Vice-President Elena thick. Concerning foreign affairs. the President toat-s that the country's relations with foreign States are friendly. He could not acquietice in the Austrian Government's request for the withdrawal of Mr. Keiley'a appointment without vioe lating his oath of office and the precepts of the Constitution, since the reasons advanced by Austria necessarily involved limitation in favour of foreign Governments upon th€ right of selection by the Americen Executive, and required much an application of a religious test as a qualification for office as would result in the practical disfranchieetnent of a large class of ciFzens, end the abandonment of the vital precepts of United States government The President centioues The force which WAS sent to the Isthmus of Panama during the late troubles was positively instructed to confine its ac- tion to efficacious protection of transit from interruption sod embarrassment. An attentive consideration of the Nicara- gua Canal Treaty leads me to withhold •submitting it to the Senate. We do not favour the policy of acquiring distant territory and the incorporation of remote interests. Our own duty at present is mainly to develop the vast resources of our great area, and to cultivate the arts of peace within our own borders, though jealously alert to prevent this hemisphere from being involved in the political problems and complications of distant Governments. I am, there- fore unable to recommend 'a proposition involving para- mount privilege*, ownership, or rights outside our territory when coupled with absolute and unlimited engagements to defend the integrity of the State where such intereets lie. While the general projects of the Nicaragua Canal is to be encouraged, I opine that a scheme entitled to favour should be free from the features mentioned. The obvious advan- tage of the Chuntepec Ship Railway, if feasible, deserves consideration. An engagement combining, construction. ownership, and working of any highway by America, with an offensive and defensive alliarce for its protection with foreign States, whose responsibilities and rights we should share, would ba inconsistent with dedication to universal neutral use, and would entail measures ler its realisa- tion beyond the scope of our national polity tend present means. SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. VANDERBILT. Newir Youx, WEDNESDAT.—AIIHJSt 'tip to the last mo- ment Mr. Vanderbilt appeared to be in excellent health. and was discussing business. with Mr. Garrett, President of the Baltimore and Ohio Railway. Great excitement prevails in the leading hotels, and late into the night railway brokers were eagerly canvassing the Prospect of te-day's stocks. Prominent capitalists. including Mr. Jay Gould and Mr. Sage, are of opinion that the market will not be seriously or permanently affected by Mr. Vanderbilt's death. At a conference of capitalists interested in the Trunk line it , was decided to purchase 200,000 shares on a declining scale. Mr. Depew, President of the New York Central Railway, declares that the death of Mr. Vanderbilt will not , alter the management of that system.

Villhrn H. Vanderbilt, who had attained the age of about 54 or 55 years, was the second on of "Commodore Vanderbilt,' Lis father, who left a fortune estimated at 20 millions sterling, having te.gun life as a tisherman. The younger Vanderbilt is stated to have died worth over 30 millions sterling. . -

Going to her house, Thomas found another coloured sea- man there., and invited him to a public-house. The woman accompanied them, and on arriving there he shot her dead. A drop of Elf t. was allowed, and death was instantaneous. The culprit previously observed that he hoped young men would be warned by his fate. for setting fire to a woman -named Agnes Welsh, was brought up in custody. The depositions of the woman were taken. She said that Titherington seized the cAndle, which she had in ber band, and threw it at her, and it set her

SERIOUS DISTURBANCE' BETWEEN IRISRISEN AND WELSH- ED/N.—OR Tuesday A serious disturbance took place at Plaspower Colliery, near Wrexham, among Irish and Welsh workmen. It is alleged that on Saturday night a number of Llishmen pelted the Welshmen with mud, stones, and pieces of glass as they were walking in procession through Wrexham. They smashed a big drum _and forcibly took away several torches. On.Tueetiay morning, by way of re- venge, the Welshmen, armed with sticks, kc ,prevented the Irishmen .from working at rlasnower, and also, it is report- ed, at Gatewn, another large colliery, several were injured. One man had several centused wourds on the head, the skin torn off the ear, slid injuries inflicted en the chest, loins, and shoulders. 11.WIIIING RAILWAY ;ACCIDENT AT LEEDB.—A serious accident occurredittlMidland Railway Station, Leeds, on Tuesday rnornisg. Thipassenger train from Norman- ton due at 2-15, ran with great force into the permanent buffers on the No. 4 platform. The buffers were thrown fully two yards back, the iron railings t /fisted, and the earthwnrk and heavy flags lifted up together. The perma- nent way is coneiderobly damaged. The engine, which was a very powerful oneocas only slightly injured. Only a few passengers arrived by the train, and so far as ascer- tained only ,one complained of serious injury; but the shock toothe others must have been severe. No definite cause can be assigned at present for the accident but either the breaks refus4 to let with efficiency in coo. sequence of the slippery state of the metals, or the driver miscalculated the distance-in pulling the train up. - -

Twa DEPTH Or THE ATLANTIC.--The depth ef the At- lantic has been sounded •, the shallowest accessible part of the ocean is in northergslatitudes. Between Newfoundland and Valentia. over what is called the telegraph plateau, the eubmariae plain extends for 140 miles without reaching the depth of 1,000 feet; then it begins to fall rapidly and goes dawn (Os lower terrace of 9,000 feet. After a little it drops to a lower plain, baying a depth of 12,000 to 14,000 feet, which stretches without variation 1,700 miles across the Atlantic_ Within 130 miles of the Irish coast it ascends by similar steps to the level of the plateau on which rests the British Islendia. Coming south from Newfounland, 200 miles from Cape Race. we cross the great bank, where the depth never exceeds 600 feet. Leaving this we plunge by a series of steps to the deepest part of the North Atlantic, with soundings of 25,000 to 30.000 feet. MR. JOHN BRIGHT ON INDIA.—Mr. Bright presided at A meeting in Birmingham on Monday evening, to hear ad- dresses from Indian gentlemen who are visiting this country in order to influence public opinion with reference to reforms in their native land, and he made a speech on our Indian Empire. He said that all that the delegates asked for was that measure of justice and tight which Governments in all ages and enuntries had owed, but had very seldom granted, to the nations under their rule. India must no longer be treated as a mere pasture ground for young Englishmen. Natives must be psrmitted to enter more largely into the Government service. England must learn the lesson that her absolute rule in her Asiatic Empire was only temporary, and that its duration depended more on wisdom than on force. He favoured the division of India into smaller presi- dencies, more nearly measured by the number of nations in Hindestan. so that if cur rule came to an end there these units might become nations, possibly confederated into the United States of mdii, instead of being embroiled in conflict one with another. The Indiana problem was crying out for solution. EsTABLISITED NEARLY 50 YEARS, White's Celebrated Moe-Main Trusses. White cud Co. have not any Agents.—Advt. A. BRAVE Marnau.—A few miles from Marlboro, near Baltimore, is a chasm spanned by an open trestle bridge, about 60 feet high. Recently, aa a pasieenger train sped round the curve nearing the bridge, the engineer was horn- to see a woman crossing it on the railway track, carrying in her arms an infant, and leading by the hand a child of per- haps three years. The engineer at once applied* the air - breaks and blew the danger signals. She heard the train approaching. turned, and looked at it, and saw the horror of her situation in nne quick glance. To jump from the bridge would he to find death in ibe wa'er ; to remain where she was a few seconds longer would be to meet instant death. Several persons near the track at the time, made signs to the engineer to stop, but he was powerless. al- though be struggled until the sweat stood Out in great drops from every pore. Then be rushed fceivard toward the front of the locomotive with the int•ntion of essaying the daring feat of seizing, the woman and dragging her to cowcatcher. At this moment the wOman caught both chil- dren in one arm. With the other she firmly seivd one of the ties on which the track is laid. and swung herself be- tween the ties below the bridge, and the train pissed over her. As soon as the train could be stopped, the conductor and breaksman rushed back to th spot where the woman was seen to disappear. They found her clinging to the ties with one arm and holding her two little ones with the other. From this perilous position they were soon rescued. LORD HARMINOTON ON THE CONSERVATIVE PARTY.— On Saturday, Lord Hartington atten led a meeting in the Pavilion at Matlock Bath, in sermon of the candicditure of his brother, Lord Edward Cavendish, for the Wewern Divi- sion of Derbyshire. Lord Edward Cavendish proposed, and Sir A. Base seconded, a resolution of confidence in the leaders of tbe Liberal party, which was darried with great enthusiasm. Lord Hartington, on risini . to respond, was loudly cheered. Be said the Conservatives had altogether refrained from repudiating the denunciations hurled be Mr. Parnell at the late Government, and by the complicity of their silence they had associated themselves with Mr. Par- nell in the charges which he had brought against the Literal party and the Executive Government of Ireland. (Cheers.) VVhat was the attitude of the Tory party to be on the other great questions that were to occupy the attention of the neat Parliament What had become of the Newport Pro- gramme of Lord Salisbury? lie (Lord riattington) ven- ture to say soon after the Newport speech that if the policy sketched in it received the support of tire party, it would indeed indicate a large sidearm,. in the principles of the Con- servative party. But he doubted whether the Tories would have the will, even if they had the power, to carry into ex- ecution the, very moderate programme sketched by Lord Salisbury. Referring to the Action if the clergy during the election, Lord Hartington ecndemned the course they bad taken as most unwise in precedent. The clergy ami the Liberation Society, though actuated by widely divergent views, were effecting the same purpose, for whilst the ono was trying to drive Liberals out of the Church, the other was trying to drive Churchmen out of the Liberal party. PROPOSED /41M RAILWAY-On Thursday morning thei scheme of the promoters of the proposed railway between Accrington, Clayton-le-Moore, Satelen, and Clitliesoe we r considered by the Clitheroe Town Council. LOCAL GOVERNMENT Beroem.-Sir Charles Dilke, speaking at the Central Conference of Poor-law Guareians in London, on Wednesday, expressed the conviction that definite proposals of local government reform would be placed before the House of Commons, and he would be glad to give the warmest support to the present Govern- ment in dealing with the question, which, however. • should be accompanied by a general revision of taxation. Ile favoured the making of new bodies directly without special representation of justices. THE ROYAL, AGRICULTTRAL Soctirre.-At the general meeting of the Royal Agricultural Society, on Thursday morning, it was announced that the Earl of Ravensw-rth mid bir Massey Lopes had been appointed vice-presidents in room of Sir Brandreth Gibbs and the late Sir Watkin Wynn. Bar- nacle, Messrs. W. Birchall, J. Buckley, J. Jackson. J. T. Hall, W. Newsome, R. Letgb, W. G. Ashton, .1. Fisher,. J. LOIN,. J. Ellison, E. Sycier, W. B Longt-m, J. Sadler, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).-.--Statistics: The Workhouse Master (Mr. Hale) reported that there were 467 inmates of the house. against 462 last we.., and 449 in the correspon- ding week of last year.—Christntas Dinner : On the motion of the Rev. T. Chambers, it was resolved that the dietary of the Workhouse inmates should be altered on Christmas Day in order that the inmate,s might have their usual Christ. man dinner.—Uftioa Contracts: When the minutes of the Visiting Committee carve \forward fer confirmation, tbs. Clerk remarked that he thought that an opportune time to discuss the advisability of limiting the acceptance of 0011... tracts to tradesmen within the Union.—Mr Bit cball there- upon moved a resolution to that effect. He sa d they bad plenty of tradtsbmen in the Union, resident at l'rescot, Widnes, St. Helens and other places quite able to supply them with prbviaions, as cheap as going to, Liverpool for them. There had been several complaints made on that subject, and if there was any benefit the ratepayers should. have that benefit. (Hear, hear) —Mr. Jackson seconded. the motion.—Tbe Clerk remarked that the resolution was The Guardians should reserve really wrong in principle. to themselves the right of acc..pting or rejecting all tenders, and when tenders were considered they could say whether they would go beyond the Union or not. He thought the res,ltition woald be improper, and if contracts were limited to tradeamen in the Union there woutt he lea' competition and ecnsequently the Guardians would base to pay higher prices for their supplies.—The Rev. T. Chambets said it appeared to him that the Guardians were right , ill principle. So long as the tradesmen of ths uilica ' could supply them there was no necessity for them to gt, outside. If there was anything to be gained be thought it ought to be given to the tradesmen in the Union.—Mr. Sadler held that there would be a falling off in competi- tion if contracts were limited to thedistrict. After 50113* further discnssion, the Rev. T. Chambers moved that in future each centract should be considered on its merits, and the motion was carried.—The Water. Suppl:ltt Mr. William Longton, of Isccleston Grange, wrote that he wan prepared to supply the Guardians with an increased water supply of 6000 gallons per hour, which would be sufficient to raise the water to a height of 50 feet above the highest part of the workhouse in case of fire. Hall ex- ; ance.—lt was afterwards d. ogled that Mr. Tiralnlitla, an ex.. - pert, s.hould be asked to inqui, e into the mitter.—This waa the principal business.

div.head: EXAMINE R.
div.p: THE EXAMINE R.
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 12, 1885.

THE Elections are not yet over; but we are, so very near the end that the few contests tha' have still to take place cannot alter the tacit that the Tory party have been utterly routee. They made great sacrifices in order to they sacrificed political consistency and Pe: litical honour, and the punishment they mar ted has come swiftly. How they gloated, when, with the Parneilites at their back, the? carried Warrington and other Lancashire boroughs in the first assault! They were net, it is true, proud of their allies; they at once discounted them, and began to talk about "the full tide of Conservative reaction." Bet they shouted before they were out of the wood; it began to be seen that the voice of the nation was not that of a Tory-Parnellite and day by day during the past fortnight we have had proof Upon proof that the people of England are loyal to Liberalism, and loyal in their Llberalism to WILLIAU EWART GLAD- STONE. The Tory-Parnellite combination has broken down ; it was formidable, but it has failed ; and both parties to it stand dis- credited before the nation ; the Tories for their shameless inconsistency in allying them- selves with men they had denounced as " rebels " and " fou, fiends ; " the Parnel- lites for their black ingratitude in turning against the party which through evil and j through good report had fought and won for 'them the Battle of the Franchise. It was de- lightful, no doubt, to both parties to " the unholy Alliance" to speculate, in advancet, on the discomfiture of the Liberals ; but The gods are just, and of our pleasant vices Make instruments to plague us. The moral of the elections gives emphasi! to the lesson which, it will be remembered, ' Mr. GLADsToNE taught before the polling' commenced, namely, that there should be 3 party in power strong enough to deal with the Irish question without having to submit te:. the dictation of a minority of the House 01, Commons under the leadership of Mr. lastg". NELL. There was no hope from the first ot the Tory party being in a position after the elections to do without the Irish vote. It ar pears to have been sufficient for them if there was a chance of retaining power with it ; I and even vet that seems to be coulr ted on as their present help in time si trouble. How little that is worth will doubt' 1 less be demonstrated bebre many moat" are over. The hope of the Parnellites wal that, by throwing the whole of their weight into the Tory scale, they could so balance parties as to be able to say who should go 11P land who should go down. But the great I preponeerance in the return of Liberals hag upset their calculations; and at this moment the Tories and the Parnellites are ready te break from each other in mutual disgust. It is true the Conservatives, having no princi- ples left to conserve, will cling to the Treasury benches until they are ignominousa kicked out. They will continue ready, a,5 they have been, to shape their policy Oa, their legislation by the speeches of Liberal leaders; and, under these circumstances, a 5 they are powerless for mischief, it'maY l/e worth while for a time to hold their noses t?, the grindstone while their Parnellite "allies turn the handle. Mr. PARNELL has made up his mind that, so far as the Tories are concerned, his ganig is up. He knows that, metaphorically speak: ing, they would cut his throat at any moment when it suited their convenience, and he noel lets it be understood that the time is not Of distant when he may try to cut theirs. In all interview with a press correspondent, ,01 Saturday night last, the Irish leader said seemed to him that the neat Parliament he not last long ; " for he did "not believe ie possibithy of a Coalition Governreen Asked as to which party he expected tv settle the Irish question, he said— I expect the settlement to come from the Liberaig, assuming that they will be about equal to ttl! Tories and Nationalists combined. It would be .4 our power on their acceptance of our terms to C'n them at once a majority of 170 votes, winch, making an allowance for considerable defectl,u from their own ranks, would be amply sufficient w enable them to deal with the Irish question and every other question"; whereas the Conservatt s cannot, even with our aid, get morethanbye bare majority, and would e always hampar the action of their eighteen or nineteen followers f Ireland. It must be cold'comfort for the Tories to hear of Mr. PARNELL speaking of the possi- bility of there being a majority against them of i7O. This, of course, implies that Par- nellites will vote Liberal if they can get a • settlement of the Irish question upon their own terms. But can they? Tie.re's the rub.

We can trust Mr. GLADSTONE, whose wisdom is always conspicuous in circumstances of difficulty, not to run into the first trap which Mr. PARNELL may bait. The great leader of the Liberal party, and we may now say of the English ration, had, there is reason to be- lieve, determined before he went to Scotland the lines upon which the largest possible measure of Home Rule could be granted to Ireland consistent with the maintenance of the integrity of the empire. At his own time, and in his own way, he will make his proposals known; and we may be quite sure that they will be such as England may honestly concede and Ireland honestly accept, apart from the intervention of Mr. PARNELL. The Irish leader is playing a desperate game. but we venture to predict that, if he prove as intractable and unrea- sonable as he did in the last Parliament, he j will be balled and beaten. Tlae Tories are powerless to help him ; he confesses it, and it is a miserable confession to make after inducing tens of thousands of Irishmen to vote with Orangemen, and against their con- sciences, in the endeavour to give a majority I to "the mortal enemies of the Irish race." He would now turn to the Liberals ; but how can he expect them to receive him with open arms I' They find that he has been a great sinner in the past, and before they can trust him in the future they Will be justified in asking him to bring forth works meet for repentance. Justice to Ireland by all means; the Irishman is " a man and a brother," but it is about time that he should be made to understand that he is not also father and mother and all the wife's.relations.

• purity and perfect thetype of Herefords, which have at length gained their reputation and profit, and the demand of American buyers • recently became so great, that the p:ices ran up to figures which threatened to approach those of the most fashionable Shorthorns in their best days. The first Herefords in West Lancashire were brought by Mr. GILLESPIE, who had resided for some time in Hereford- shire. Mr. KAY, of Longridge, next introduced to his large farms on the Salisbury slopes the nucleus of a pure-bred herd, and he has latterly taken home the drafts from the best stocks in Herefordshire, and has commenced what promises to be a profitable system of ex- portation to America. On the t-_alesbury farms there are to be found two-year-old Hereford steers plump and fat, which cer- tainly cannot be said of the steers of any other breed. The prejudice amongst some butchers that Herefords do not cut up as profitably as other breeds is disappearing, for one Lancashire butcher, with a little more enterprise than his brethren, tested the merits of the breed with other classes of stock, and was soon convinced of their superiority. What Mr. GILLESPIE. suggests to those who feed stock for the shambles is that the most profitable system for them is to cross Shorthorns with Hereford bulls, and experience proves that he is right. The aim of a few of the Lancashire fan- ciers of Herefords is that the County Agri- cultural Society shall, by permitting prizes to be offered at their exhibitions for the breed named as a distinct class, encourage the introduction of a stock which, they hold, surpasses any other for beefing quail ties, and we believe the members will not I hesitate to support the proposal. There is !no doubt the department will bring fresh members and exhibitors into the Lancashire Society, and that its general tendency will be Ito the interest of cattle breeders and of the ! public. If we recollect right, the Herefords ! were tried in connection with the Cotmty , Show twelve years ago at .Chester, but only one gentleman entered stock. However, much has happened since, and with the co- operation of the Hereford Herd Book Society and kindred organisations, a grand entry may be considered certain, and we have no doubt the proposal will be cordially accepted.

Should he marry and have a family, he has to .think of making provision for the younger chil- dren. He knows that every pound he spends on his estate lessens his chance of making this provision and it thus happens that nothing is done. Hors TRINITY CHURCH, Rtmcome.—The Rev. T. C. Escott, curate of Holy Trinity Cnurch, Runcoro, has left Runcorn for Bristol. He will be succeeded by Mr. Jervis, lay helper, who is to be ordained. Tag- Lean M. THOMAS NORMAN, OF RUNCORN.— In the wina`ow of the shop of Messrs. Boyden aid Coventry, Church-street, is exhibited a capitally executed portrait in oil of the late Mr. Thomas Norman. Mr. Andrew Matthew is the artist. ST. MICEIAEL'S CHURCH. RUNCORN.—The second of the series of entertainments in aid of this church took place in the National Schoole on Thursday evening. There WAS a moderate attenclauce, and the Rev. T. M. Anima presided. An interesting programme was gone through. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—Williarn Hughes, door- keeper to the Salvation Army, was on Tuesday eveming seized with a tit of apoplexy at the shop Of Mr. T. Ly... - late, Devonshire-square. He was carried into the Foresters' Hall, where a bed was prepared for him, and he was at- tended by Drs. ktobinsoci and McDougall. Death ensued at five o'clock next morning. The deceased was 35 years of age SALE OF WORK AT RUNCORN.—With the object of aug- menting the funds of the Church Missionary Society and the Pastoral Aid Society, a sale of work was held on Thursday afterimon at Holy Trinity Schools, Runcorn. The principal stall was laden with a varied assortment of articles, the outcome of the labours of the sewing class con- ducted by Mrs. Preston, and they were dispensed to the purchasers by the same hands. Mesdames Fisher, Lea, and Whitt.ker, and Misses Stubbs and ryrie were in charge of the refreshment stall. An interesting feature was tee exhibition of eastern curiosities by Mrs. Foley, of Widnes In the evening too concerts were given. The visitors were numerous and a good sum was realised. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. Present—Messrs. W. Littler (chair- man), H. Coleburn, W. Mellor, W. H. Rogerson, E. Imi- son, R. Morris, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary) The secre- tary reported that daring the eight months ended November 25th, there had been 215 interments, a decrease of 24 Com- pared with the previous year. The amount of fees received was £220 18s, against £264 14a Id in the corresponding period of 1884. Accounts amounting to £l7 196 61 were passed for payment, and cheques for interest falling due amounting to £3l its lid were signed. At the next meet- ing the Board will consider the subject of the renewal of a lean of £250 from the Lily of the Valley Lodge of Odd- fellows. At present 4 per cent. is paid, and an opinion was expressed that not more than 31 per cent, should be paid in future. FRODSHAM AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY.-0a Thursday evening the above society gave two performances in the Tows Hall, Frodshem. There was an excellent attendance, amongst these present haing—The Vicar, Mr. 11. Reynolds and family, Mr. James Reynolds, Dr. Steel and family, Mr. A. Thomas and family, Mr. Tom Ashton, Mr. G. Ashton, Mr. W. Linaker an family, Miss West, Mr. arid Mrs. Pride, Mrs. C. Reynolds, Mr. arid Mrs. Holland (Mobberley), Mr. Hadfield and family, Mr. and Mrs. H Linaker, senr., Mrs. H. Linaker, junr , Rev. R. 51. P. Butler, Mr. C. Linaker and family, rte. The first piece was entitled "Heir at law." The acting of Mr. It. Holland, as Dick Dowlas, was excel- lent. He carried out the character to the life ; and none the less can be said of Mrs. C. E. Linaker in her represen- tation of Deborah Dowlas. Perhaps the most difficult character of the piece, and the one which calls for the most praise, was that of the worthy Doctor Panglass (Mr. E. Rhodes.) He displayed histrionic abilities of no mean order, and his acting was provocative of much mirth. The other performers carticd out their parts in an aqually satis- factory manner. The second piece was denominated "Diamond cut diamond." The good acting which charac- terized the first piece was maintained, and at the conclusion of the comedy everyone was delighted. During the evening a string bend from Runcorn played selections of music, and the audience dispersed with the" National Anthem." MILL BROW BAND CONCERT, RUNCORN. The third annual concert of the Mill Brow Brass Band to de place in the Runcorn Public Hall, on Wednesday evening. The boisterous weather militated against the success of the con- cert from a financial point of view. The audience was of very moderate proportions, but many persons who had booked seats in advance were absent, and the leSa to the promoters will not be so heavy as appearances Indicated. The performances of the band moaopolieed a large share of the programme, and although the five selections, including Mr. Charles Godfrev's arrangement of "Nabucodonosae." were executed with skill and tunefulness, a little curtail- ment was desirable. The progress made by the hand was very palpable, and the credit of their training and ability must be ascribed to the conductor Mr. Tom Outhwaite. Mr. R. W. Pierpoint gave the cornet solo " Les Folies Polka" with his usual brilliancy of execution, and he was loudly applauded. Mr. Outhwaite played with . great success euphonium solo entitled "Swiss air." His talented mani- pulation of his instrument won him unrestricted applause. The vocalists were Madame Laura Howarth and Mr. Chas. Chilley. In the first pert Madame Howarth sang " Dear bird of winter " with a power and effect which showed that her voice had lost none of its qualities. In the second part she contributed "II Bade" and " Going to the market." and in response to an enthusiastic and deserved encore, favoured the audience with "Within a mile of Edinbro' town." Mr. Chilley possesses a tenor voice of much sweet- ness and good compass, and his interpretation of "Go xl company," his first song, earned him a recall, and he re- peated the last verse. Hearty encores also rewarded him for his artistic vocalisation of "-Tom Bowling" and "Good night, beloved." Madame Howarth and Mr. Chilley In con- junction sang "Una Notte Venezia" with pretty effect. Tne concert terminate. 1 with the chores "Worthy is the lamb" from the Messiah, performed by the hand in capital style. Mr. Mozart Barton officiated as the accompanist, and Mr. Tom Outhwaite conducted the band. Winsms CHORAL SOCIETY.—The first concert of the season in connection with this society was given in Lacey- street'School.roem, on Thursday evening. It is much to be regretted that the efforts of the Choral Society do not meet with the appreciation they deserve .from the towns- people. An excellent programme of sacred and secular music had not attracted more than sufficient to balf fill the room, but the lack of numbers was compensated for to some degree by the discriminating appreciation shown by the company. Selections from Handel's " Messiah" comprised the first part of the programme. The chorus was well balanced and admirably trained ; the band performed their part with almost faultless execution, and the selections were highly eiejovable. 'l'he most conspicuous success of the chorus was 4 Unto us a child is born," but in all they I acquitted themselves in A manner that showed careful ' rehearsal. The recitative " Comfort ye, my people" and the air " Every valley ehall be exalted " were sung by Mr. Joseph Morrison with power and expression, and the hearty plaudics that greeted him were well deserved. Mr. W. G. Bevan gave the recitation "Thus saith the Lord " and the airs "But who may abide the day of His com- ing" and "The people that walked in darkness" in a ' manner that evinced careful study, and his efforts were thoroughly appreciated. With considerable effect Miss R. Greenell sang "Rejoice greatly" and " Come unto Him all ye that labour," and Mrs. Lea was very success- ful in her interpretation of the air '4 Oh thou that tellest of good tidings in Zion," while Miss Broad gave a sweet rendering of "He shall feed His flock." The pareetal symphony was a deliglatful performance by the baud. The chorus ' Hallelujah" concluded the first part, and the eecond opened with a piece of fine instrumen- tation in the Overture" Marionette." Miss H. Argent con- tributed the violin solo "Faust" with a manipulatory skill that secured her a vociferous encore, and she responded. For her able interpretation' of Rossini's "Uric voce puce ga" Miss.Greenall also was recalled. Mr. Eustree Carey sang the song " When in dark mid-night" to the evident pleasure of the audience, and Mr. Morrison at a moment's notice contribut-d "The angel at the window," which be sang with expressive power. Several choruses were given in lice style, and the proceedings concluded with 'the "National Anthem." Mr. W. L Argent conducted with his accustomed ability and success.

RELAPSE OF THE DEAN OF CHESTER. —At ele- °Tam has been received at the Deanery, Chester, from Bournemouth, stating that Dr. Howson has had a serious relapse, and now lies in a very criti- cal condition. Mrs llowson is still under medical attention at Chester for' a fractured leg. THE NORTIIWICH RIOTS.—The police have issued twenty summonses against persons alleged to have been concerned in the riots at Northwich. These persons are all charged with wilful damage and also with riotous conduct, and one of them with assault- ing the police. One man, it is alleged, had his head cut open by a policeman's truncheon as he stood at his own door.

• A GOOD LANDLORD.—Lord Tollemache, who for two months past has been staying at Peckforton Castle, Cheshire, celebrated his 80th birthday on _Monday. His lordship has completely recovered from the serious illness which he passed through al Ishort time since, and is again able to personally attend to the improvements which he is constantly making on the l'eckforton estate. Lord Tollemache possesses about 46,000 acres of land in Cheshire, and lit is a most striking testimony to the value of his supervision that during the whole of the agricul- tural depression from 1877 to 1885 he has had neither a vacant farm nor a tenant in arrears. his estate in Cheshire has during his lifetime been cut up into sizeable farms of about 200 acres in extent, his lordship considering that a thrifty farmer with sons and daughters could do excellently on a 200- acre farm, but not on a smaller holding. In order to break up his estate into farms of that size he built or rebuilt between fifty and sixty farmhouses at the enormous cost of £148,000. Each of these farms or homesteads costs £2,800. In addition to this Lord Tollemache has built no fewer than 260 cottages for the accommodation of his labourers, and thus satisfactorily solved the labour difficulty on the Peckfortan estate. Lord Tollemache was anxious to provide mixed schools for the education of the farmers' and labourers children, but after the schools had been built, he found that the far, mers objected to send their sons to the same schools with the labourers' children. Having listened to the masters' complaint, his lordship said, "There is only one way out of the difficulty; I will send my own sons to the school," and for nearly two years Lord Tollemache's children attended the school; "and,' he adds, in referring to the matter, "to their undoubted advantage.''

ANTZ-VAECINATION.—On Wednesday afternoon eleven additional summonses were served on per- sons in Earlestown who had failed to have their children vaccinated. There are seven defendants, and the cases will be heard at the Newton Petty Sessions to-day (Saturday.) THE HOME IRON Ti.—A more hopeful feel- ing is beginning to prevail in the English irbn mar- ket, and although this is not justified by a growth in actual requirements, yet the despondency of re- cent times appears to be lifting off the trade. The Glasgow warrant market, it is Irue, has gone flat again, and the hopefulness of the last few weeks has disappeared, the slackness in thh American and continental demand being the principal cause of the depression. Scotch makers are not doing much, and prices are easier. In the North of England pig- iron trade, on the contrary, there is an enlarged de- mand for delivery of pig iron next year, and buyers are ready to pay is. per ton more than the present rates for delivery from January to June. In Lanca- shire makers are also firm in their prices for pig iron, and hematites have improved there 2.5. per ton. In the north-west of England the improved tone in the hematite iron trade is also maintained, makers being sold well forward, whilst stocks are decreasing.—lron. •

• A CHE-SHIRE CLERGYMAN AND PRAYERS FOR THE DEAD.—The Rector of Coppenhall (Crewe) having been asked to contradict a statement that he had affixed to the notice board in his church the request, "Of thy mercy pray for the repose of the soul of the Rev. J. B. Whteler" (one of his prede- cessors), has written to a correspondent as fol- lows :—.‘ Dear sir,—The statement to which you refer was substantially correct. 1 boldly teach the duty of praying for the departed, and publicly ask for the suffrages of the faithful on their behalf. I 'utterly deny that my practice is Roman,' unless, indeed, we are prepared to make the Roman Cathol- ics a present of the fathers of the undivided Church. The Church of England has suffered many things through the mutilation, or suppression of truth, but she can never receive 'damage' by the preaching of the whole counsel of God.—l am, dear air, yours vezy truly in the faith of Him who is Lord both of the dead and living, Witusix CAWLEY REID, Cop- penhall Rectory, Crewe."

MANCHESTRIL SHIP CANAL—At a meeting of the Board of Directors, held at the offices, 70, Market- street, Manchester, on .Tuesday afternoon, the .engineer, Mr. E. Leader Williams, reported that trial shafts were being sunk on the line of the Canal between Eastham and Runcorn, and that prepara- tions were being made to sink similar shafts near Manchester. Mr. Williams was instructed to stake out the centre line of the whole length of the canal for the inspection and approval of the directors. A London correspondent says un- derstand that up to the present time the amount of share capital subscribed for the Manchester Ship Canal is about £1,000,000, but of course no serious effort will be made to obtain the total amount re- quired until the bill now before Parliament author- ising the payment of interest out Of capital has been passed. Before the promoters could reasan-' ably ask for such a power it was, however, neces- sary that they should attempt to raise•the money, and having done so4.hey will be fully entitled to go before Parliament, appealing, on the same grounds as did the Hull and Barnsley Railway Company, that the Standing Orders forbidding the payment of interest during construction may be snspended, in order that the great work contemplated in the bill shall not be frustrated.

THE LATE BISHOP OF kANpIIESTER,-011 Mon- day a meeting, largely attended by clergymen and others, was held at the Gentlemen's Concert Hall, Manchester, for the purpose of discussing the pro- ject of a memorial to the late Bishop of Manches- ter. Lord Winmarleigh presided, and was suppor- ted by the Dean of Manchester, the Archdeacon of Manchester, the Rev. Canon Kelly, Mr. E. Hard- castle, M.P.; Mr. W. E. M. Tomlinson, M.P.•, Mr. G. Milner, Mr. G. W. Maclure, the Rev. .1. E. Gull, and other gentlemen.—The Chairman stated that it was suggested to place the proposed statue in the north end of the cathedral near the chair. His lordship then went on to describe in a few words the noble work the late Bishop had done for the vast diocese which was under his charge. He (the chairman) had groat pleasure in moving the following resolu- tion :--" That it is desirable, that a suitable monu- ment to the late Bishop be erected in his own cathedral church as a memorial of his episcopate." —The resoldion was seconded by Mr. Tomlinson, M.P.—Mr. E. Hardcastle, M.P. who supported the resolution, further moved tillit the monument should be in the shape of a recumbent effigy, and that the place on which it shoed be erected be left to the decision of. the Dean and Chapter, and the committee to be hdreafter elected.,

THE POLITICAL SITUATION.—Mr. Gladstone has had lengthy conferences at Hawarden, first with Lord Granville and subsequently with Lords Rose- bery and Spencer. A London Liberal contemporary announced on Wednesday that Lord Salisbury, "re- cognising the position," had" abandoned all inten- tion of attempting to conciliate the Irishk vote." His policy, added the Daily News, "will now be directed towards affecting an alliance with the 'moderate Liberals,' and resisting the anticipated demands of Mr. Parnell." On this the Globe remarks that" nobody knows, or can possibly know, what course her Majesty's Ministers intend to take in an unprecedented crisis." Ministers meet on Monday, and they will then determine their course. The St. James's Gazette asks, will the endeavour to make terms with the "moderate Liberals" succeed? Our contemporary prepares the Conservatives for disap- pointment. Mr. Gladstone, it says, will take up the position that the offer of an alliance should come, not from the Conservatives to the Liberals, but from the Liberals to the Conservatives, the condi- tion precedent being that the Conservatives, as the weaker party, should vacate the Treasury bench. Parliament meets on the 12th i January ; but it is not expected that the Queen will take part in the ceremony. It is thought that after the transaction of formal business, the House will adjourn till the usual meeting in February. Earl Spenfter, who met the Earl of Rosebury at Hawarden Castle by ar- rangement, left on Thursday for London, travelling by the ten o'clock express from Chester. Mr. Glad- stone is in the enjoyment of excellent health. In a letter to Lord William Compton, congratulating him on his election for the §tratford-on-Avon divi- sion of Warwickshire, Mr. Gladstone says :—" A wonderful election. It will prove, I think, that we have decidedly gained, on the Tories since 1880, if allowance be mode for the balance of five seats given them through double candidatures, and for' fifteen seats, a very moderate estimate, given them by Mr. Parnell."

WARRINGTON AND WIDNES CIRCUIT OF WESLEY- ANS.—The quarterly meeting of this station was held on Saturday at Widnes. The Circuit Sunday school Committee met after dinner and transacted business in connection with the Sabbath schools, and made arrangements for the Rev. T. Whittaker to visit the schools at Warrington, Widnes, and Sims Cross ; to hold special services at each Of these places, with a Conference of teachers. The schools were tound to be in a flourishing con- dition. At 2-30 the preachers' meeting commenced; the Rev. J. Calvert; president; Bro. S. Owens, secretary; and Bro. S. Draught, assistant secretary. There was a good number of preachers present and taking part. Not a single complaint was made of the preachers not fulfilling their appointment, which speaks well for the efficient mode of work- ing the • various societies in the circuit. , Arrangements were made to bring out some young pen who are to accompany the elder brethren to their appointments and to take part therein, and the other orders of business being attended to, the full board commenced its sittings at three o'clock, when there was a large attendance. The requests from the societies were considered and attended to, and arrangements made for special services during the coming quarter. The circuit accounts were found to be in a very satisfactory state, and the circuit is in a much more prosperous state than ever it was before. The attendance at the chapels has greatly improved; there is an increase of members, and after paying all expenses, minister's salary, &c., there is a good balance in hand. Circuit Stemard T. Rollison, Esq., was re-appointed, and the other circuit officials were re-instated, and the highly esteemed minister, the Rev. J. Calvert, was cordially invited, and consented, to stay in this sta- tion a third year. A resolution was passed to send letters of congratulation to the four officials in the connexion who have attained to thd honour of being representatives in Parliament, and aletter of sym- pathy to the Rev. W. Malalien, who is very heavily afflicted, and who was formerly superintendent of the circuit.

REVIVAL IN THE CIIESHIRR SALT TRADE.—The great Cheshire salt industry, which has been much depressed for some years, shows every indication of reviving, the exports for November from the Mer- sey, via the Weaver river, being 90,183 tons, against 76,463 tons for the corresoonding month of last year. Our best customer is the East Indies, which took 36,433 tons in November alone. CHRISTMAS AND NEW YEAR CARDS.—A large selection of cards for the present season, including the choicest specimens of the lithographic and ' photographic arts, is now on view at Mr. John S. Green's, 34, Bridge-street, Warrington. There is also a charming display of the latest novelties in hand-Psinted cards, water colours, etchings, mirrors, i &c., which all readers of the Examiner would do well to inspect. —Advt. Mn. JOHN RIGBY, Q.C.—Mr. John Rigby, who has carried the Wisbech division of Cambridgeshire in the interest of the Liberal party, has many friends in this neighbourhood, and was educated at the College in Liverpool. Mr. Rigby is a Queen's Counsel, and one of the most eminent practitioners at the Chancery Bar. He is a cousin of Mr. F. Rigby, J.P., of Frodsham, and was born at Riincorn, upon which town he reflects the highest honour.

The Rev. Jams Jones Bryant, Vicar of Lower Whitley, folmerly of Weston Point, .aued Mr. Frederick Savage, farmer, Pickow Farm, Runcorn, for 119 158 damages for alleged breach of wartanty on the sale of a: mare.—Mr. F. A. Lake represented the plaintiff, and Mr. A. F etcher, of Notthwich, detended.—The plaintiff said prior to the 13th Septemb-r he SSW the pony. Tne defendant then stated it was very quiet, went quietly in harness, alt the members of hie family had driven it, and his (witness's) wife might drive him. On the Bth October he saw the animal run up and down the yard, arid inf•rtned defendant he would lot him known in a day or two if he would buy It. On the following day be again visited the farm, and told the defen- dant, "1 have come to buy the horse limn you, as the son of your father." He added." Do you know anything about the mare?" The defendant replied," No. All I know of her is that she formerly went in a grocer's cart." As far as he knew, the dehndant afterwards said, the mare was all right, and he (witnese) could have her examined by a veterinary sureeon. Mr. Bryant said he would take his word, and wrote out a cheque for £24. No receipt was given. After the gale was completed, witness remarked that horses were very diseereeable. His brother when he sold horses would never sell one to a friend, and never give a warranty. The mare WAS delivered on tbe 10th October. sod between two and three on the eain• day be drove tier to Higher RUDCAID, a distence of shout 31 miles. She weut indifferently, and become lame. On Sunday he drove her to Whitley, a distance of 16 miles there and back for two services. She went very lame, especially coming down hill. He afterwards ascertained that she was hopelessly lame, ant on the 14th Oct. be sent her back to defendant, who refused to receive her. He afterwafds had the animal sold by auction for £7.—Johu Beckett, a youth who. had groomed the horse, and William Whitby, the weigher, of West in Point, who looked after Captain Clark's stables where the mare was kept, corroborated am to the lamenerie.—eie S Yarwood, veterinary surgeon, deposed that he examined the animal on the 16th October. She was very lame ;suffering from a very bad sprain of long standing. On the 28th Oct. he again examined the horse in conjuaction with ;qr. J. Kirby Pilkington, veterinary surgeon, Everton-brow, Liver- pool. They came to the same conclusion.—Mr. Pilkingi ton corroborated.—Mr. Luke Holmes. auctioneer, proved the sale of the mare.—Mr. Fletcher asked for a verdict on the ground that the words used by the defendant did not consti- tute a warranty, and that there was no proof that tee de- fendant knew of the mare's lamenees.—Mr. Lake argued against this contention.—His benour, after a few minutes deliberation, said he would hear the evidence for the de- fence.—Mr. F. Savage, the defendant, said he occasionally bought and sold horses. Ile narrated how the plaintiff came to his farm and asked to see the mere. He told him she was doing Work for his father, out would send for her. He did se and she was trotted several times up anti down the road. The plaintiff felt her hocks, and found some fault with them. He asked if she was all right, and he (defendant) replied that she was so far as he knew, but as he did not profess to be a veterin try surgeon he could nit say if she were sound or not. He told Mr. Bryant that If he was not perfectly satisaed in his own judgment he could get her examined by any qualified man, but he would not have a quack. After this Mr. Bryant again examined her and asked her price. He replied £25. Tbe next day Mr. Bryant came to the farm again, and said he would give £24 for the mare. Ile replied "We shan't fall out for a sovereign ; you shall have her." He asked Mr. Bryant if he had seen the mars Out that morning, and be answered that he could judge a horse better in the stable than outside They no burned to the °dice, where in course of conversation Mr. Bryant said "I cannot expect a warranty. I had a brother in Wales who sold horses. He got good prices for them, and he always made a point of two things—he never sold a horse with a warranty and never sold a horse to a friend." Mr. BrYant then handed him a cheque. He (witnesa) bought the mare at Chester July fair. She Was not then breken to harness. He broke her, and there were no symptoms of lameness or of sprain. Almost every day she took out meat for his father in a shandry. In cross-examinalon he said he had driven the mare long distances. He bought horses to sell again, but he did not patch up broken down horsea.—Samuel Davies, blacksmith, Runcorn, said he saw the mare as often as once a week. She bad been shoed at his place frequently, and he never saw her lame.—Alfred Watkin deposed that he shoed the animal for the plaintiff, and there was no complaint made that she was lame. He had seen her often and never saw her lame.—His Honour gave judgment for ,the defendant, and against the plain- tiff. CAUTION TO FINDERS OF STRAY DOGS.—An action Was brought by William Cheshire, boatman, of Lowlands-road. Runcorn, against Joseph Jolley, labourer, Norton•etreet. foG 30. i, value of a fox terrier hitch detained.—Mr. Hitchen ap- peared for the plaintiff.—The defendant admitted that he had the dog, hut had refused to give it up to plaintiff un- til he had been paid the coat of an advertisement and for the keep of the dog during the time it was in his poseession. His honour said the defendant was bound to give the dog up to the plaintiff, and trust to the plaintiff's honour to pay him the amount be had expended. He (the judge) would certainly have paid for the advertisement and the keep of the animal. It was a very common notion amongst people that if they found a dog they had notning to do but adver- tise the fact, and make the owner pay. This was quite wrong. Any one fieding a dog ought to take it to the police office and let the matter rest there.—His Honour awarded the damages claimed, the amount to be reduced to Is if the dog was returned in a week.

NEGLECT OF A CHILD.

. On Monday afternoon, at the Sessions House, Mr. I'. J. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquiry touching tSe death of Mane Lowe, eight years of age, daughter of Stephen Lowe, chemical labourer, 49, Ileath-road. Superintendent Leah represented the notice and Mr. W. H. Linaker the Guar- dians.—The Coroner said the cause for holding the inquiry was a trifle peculiar. The child died on the 3rd December, an Dr. Mangan, who seemed to haws seen the child, gave a certificate of death. The do or's certificate wiis taken to the reg:etrar, and Mr. Colebnrn registered the death. But sometime on the 4th December the registrar wrote to Super- intendent Leah a letter, from which the following was an extract Mr. James Percival, inspector of nuisanc.s, called upon me this afternoon, and informed me that a child of the name of Maria Lowe, aged eight years. died yesterday at 49, I:Leath-road, Runcorn, and that Dr. MacDougall

Iwished me not to register the death until an inquiry had been made as t . the cause of death. I don't know anythieg about the care myself, but Dr. MacDougall most have a sufficient reason to send such a message to me." In a further letter from Messrs. Neva and Creaswell it was stated that unless after the meeting ne the 8:13 inst. the ex- penses to which their client had been put had keen re. pail they would bike legal proceedmas to enforce it.—This correspondence was laid on the table. .

INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL FOR WIDNES INTERESTING FIGURES. Yesterday afternoon Mr. S:epheu Hardiog Terry', an inspector to the Local Government B ard, held an in- quiry at the offices of the Widnes Local Board into the application of the Board for sanction to borrow £4,000 for the purpose of providing an infectious diseases hospital. There were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. J. Taylor, D. Wright, B. Dutton, F. Beyer', J. Doughton. Sadler, D. Huret, J. T. Allen (clerk), W. Higginson (surveyor), J. Dickson (insurance inspector).—The Clerk said the Board were under the necessity by the regulations of the Local Govarnment Board to provide hospital accommodatiott for any outbreak of infectious disease that might occur. Un- fortunately they were unable to combine with any other authority in dealing with cases. The workhouse was the. nearest place. but the provisions of the Guardians wets 80 strict that the Board could not depend upott them taking any ca.es the Board m'ght have in the district. At the same time he must say tkat a. far as Widnes was concerned they bad very little to fear. From 1880 to 1885 the death-rate from zymntic disease in the township had. averaged from .9 to 4-77. That he thought WAS a very' low rate.—The In.pector What is your total deathrate.—Dr. O'Kveffe : Last month 1288. If averages about 13 for the year.—The Clerk (continuing) said in 1883.84 there was a serious outbreak of smallpox. There were io all 32 cases, and Rix of the sufferers died.— The Inspector remarked that it WO very inconvenient hay- ing arrangements with other Anthorities.—The Clerk said that WAS one reason why the ' Local Board bad decided to , treat their own cases. The Baud had Applied for power to borrow £4 000, but he nnierstood that it was not intended to spend that amount at present. On the tteneral district rate they bad power to borrow about £70,000. They had , borrowed and spent £51,000. The annual repayments of I principal and interest of this sum amounted to £3 003, and this was equal to a rate of 711 in the L. In addition, the Board had authority to borrow £BOO for land for the hospi- tal. He, however, thought the Board would not borrow that sum. They would, he was Of opinion, agree with him that they could find that money out of 4, special fund thee had in band. Upsn public offices they had power to borrow £5,500, and that amount would be required. Then to cornplete the main sewer he estimated

1 they would need another instalmmt of £5,000, and noW' g they asked for £4,000 for the lefectinua Diseases Hospital. a That made a total of £17,000. To repay that in 30 years s at 4 per cent meant £1,012 a year, equ ato a rate of 2id in - the X. That added to the 7d to which they were already - committed made a rate of 101 in the X on general district • rate for public improvements. For the past year the general district rate, inclasive of the VA he had mentioned, had been 23 in the X. The poor rate WAS also 2s, making the total rates of the township 48 in the C.—The Inspector said this could not be considered a high rate in a district where great and important public works had been corn. plated, and othQrs were in progress.—Dr. O'Keeffe said the hospital would be a great boon to the township, awl be de- scribed the great difficulties under which the Board laboured on the outbreak of small-pox in 1883. He pointed out that in the proposed building provision had been made for the separation of the sexes, and they could treat three separate diseases.—Tbe Inspector Observed that the building was no arranged that it could easily be added to.— In reply to Mr. T. Sadler, Dr. O'Keeffe said it was only in- tended t 3 spend at the present time £2,000, and the Clerk observed that the annual expense would depend upon the disease they had in the township.—The Inspector : If there is no outbreak of disease the expenditure will be met out of the preeent rates. If an outbreak .1 discus's occurs you will be justified in spending money to tramp out this disease, and it will in the end he the cheapest thing you can do,— answering Mr. Dutton, the Clark said the annual expense of the hospital would be about £lOO, which would not mean a farthing on the rates —Mr. T. Sadler: I am perfectly satiefied.-Mr. Higginson then described the plans, with which readers of the Examiner are familiar, and sal accommoda- tion WAS provided for tee persons, but they could accommo- date double the number in the same rooms if necessary.... The Inspector said the plans did their surveyor great credit, and to the auteority for bringing them forward.—The in. quiry then conciaded.
