A SUSPICIOUS CASE.—The Assistant Clerk referred to the case of a child which had died at Runcorn under some- what suspicious circumstances. Tbe Baerd'n officer, Mn Ward, had made inquiries about tte cbtld the previotui week, and he told Lim (the assistant clerk) that the child was net being properly cared for, aud he told the officer that the best thing that could be done was to take the child to the Workhouse, On Friday, however, be received infor- mation that the cbild was dead and the next morning be ascertained from toe superinteudent of pe:ice that a medi- cal certificate bad been given that the child had died from consumption. Under the circumstauces, however, he took it upon himself to notify the coroner, and the medical offi- cer of the Uoion sent word to the registrar not to register the death. An inquest bad accordingly been held on the previous day the report of which appeared in the sews- papers—The Rev. J. Lockwood said the coroner in hie re- marks justified the action Mr. Linaker had taken.—The Assistant Clerk said that the evidence the Board's officer gave at the isquest seemed to differ fro:n the information that was given to him, and he suggested that the officers should each keep a diary of their proceedings—Mr. Speak. lean moved, and Mr. Aaron seconded a proposal that the ofiSeers be requested to keep a diary, and it was agreed to. . A BE.CEMaKER'S CrA Longton- appeared in a case in which Charles Longshaw, brickmaker, of Lvarna carrying on business at Warrington, sued Henry Litherland, also a brickmaker, for £25 12s 41, being £l3 2s damages for bad work and £l2 103 41 for money overpaid.—Mr. Longton, in stating the case for the plaintiff, said that in February of 1835, the plaintiff and defendant had a con. versation as to the latter undertaking a contract for brick- making for plaintiff during the season of 1835. Defendant wrote offering to make bricks at Sankey for 1.03 91 per 1,000 counted from the flats, or at lie 6.1 per 1,090 counted from the kiln, to draw on account monthly, and settle up at the eed of the season. Plaintiff agreed to the terms of lie 61 per 1,000 bricks. and defendant proceeded with the c-ntract. On March 14th he drew £l3 on account, for which he gave a receipt, ana from time to time he received payments on account amounting to £llO 103. All went right until the first of Angust, when defendant had one particular kiln in course of burning. Plaintiff visited defendant on that day, a Satur- day, and paid him a large amount of money, and on the same day defendant loft his work and broke up the contract. When plaintiff no the following Monday went to the kiln there was no sane there, and much damage had in conaequence resulted. Plaintiff managed to dispose of earns of the bricks, and for them had allowed defendant lie 6d per 1,000. He claimed for the amount that be maid not dispose of in consequence of the damage, a email sum for countim,-, and the amount stated as overpaid—The defendant, who was sof, represented, contended that the plaintiff was bound under the c mtract to snpply all the materials necessary for the making ot bricks, and that at the kiln in question the plaintiff had failed to supply stock, although requested to do so, for the purpose of roofing and burning the kiln. Defendant said that small coal would not do as well as slack, as it would " cinder " instead of burning, and that slack was essentially necessary for the successful burning of the kiln in question.—liis Honour said that even Were that the case it did not justify defend- ant in leaving work as he appeared to have done. He gave judgment for £9, which, as far as could be properly &seer- rained, was the amount of damage that bad been caused. A Losr Don. William Davison brought an action against Richard Stathert for the return of a Bisset honed dog or ita value. Mr. H. J. Longton appeared for the plain- tiff and the defendant appeared in [serene. Toe dog had been sent on approval, but had been lost by defen tent, who now appeared and offered £2 and the costs, which was ac- cepted. UNEXPECTED "TRICK" OF A PERFORMING PONY.—Ia this cage Mr. Jenkins appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Dobson defended. The claim was for £O, for damages for injuries sustained by the plaintiff at Great Sankey, on the. 16th of August. through alleged negligence in insecurely fastening a pony to a gate in the yard of the Chapel House Inn, Great Sankey, whereby the pony broke loose. A special jury was empannelled to try the issue. Defendant, Frederick Ginnett, was alleged to be a circus proprietor, of Belfast ; and the plaintiff was James Wright, farmer, Caerdley Farm, Great Sankey. On Sunday morning, the 16th August, a man drove up to the Chapel House inn, which is kept by Thomas Baxter, and requested to be allowed to water a number of horses. Permission was given, and shortly after a number ef horses, elephants' and other accessories to a circus drove up at the inn. The bulk of the horses were fed by means of portable mangers, but a pony, five years old, was fastened to a wicket-gate in the- yard of the inn. It was an entire pony. About a "quarter- past ten o'?.lock Mr. Davies, an estate agent, of Widnes, drew up to the yard in a waggonette, accompanied by other persons, who were going to service at Sankey Church. Shortly afterwards the plaintiff drove into the yard in a gig, accompauied by lis wife and two children. After assisting them to alight? plaintiff proceeded to fasten the reins to the harness, before taking the horse out, and as he was moving towards the bead of his mare, the pony, which it was assumed was fastened to the wicket gate, turned round soddenly and made a rush at the mare, nlung- jag with its forelegs. The mare reared up, the result being that the pony knocked Mr. Wright down, and fell upon him. Mr. Davies rushed to the mare's head, and received a blow, but extricated the mare, which rushed to the other rnd of the yard, and tried to get throngs a fence, but w ithout suc- cess. A man in the employ of the defendant laid hold d the pony, took it away, and made a remark to the effect h "be knew they weld(' have some accident with the little devil if they were not careful." That went to show that it was known that the pony was dargerous, and it was, there- fore, incumbent on the defendant to have some person in charge of it. Plaintiff did not ask for sentimental damages, hut for such as the jury plight consider reasonable. Plain- tiff was injured about the body. The injuries did net re— quite a great deal of medicine; brit this accident happening in the month of kugust, at a time when it was most essential that a farmer should be attending to his duties and also to the markets, had had a considerable effect upon him financially, as he was unable to attend to his business for some weeks.— Mr. Dobson, for the defence, said the defendant nas not the owner of the circus, but belonged to the pony, Which WAS lent to the proprietor of the oircne.—Fred le ar ui cdk was then examined, and said he,was a circus rider and borne trainer. He was employed by his brother, c who was at the present time proprietor of the ercus. The pony belonged to witness, bale had no sbrvant to look after it. The cirms was conducted under the name of Frederick Ginnetr. but that was the name of witness'e grand- father, ;I‘nd the name was retained to distinguish th, circus from thnife of other persons named Oinnett.-Mr. Jenkins asked his Honour to amend the summons, aud that it should be made out in the name of Claud GI/meta—His Honour said he was sorry there were difficulties in the way of deciding the case that day. Althosgh the defendant's earns was Frederick Ginnett, there was no evidence to ehow that he was the proprietor of the circus. There seemed to' have been a mistake ir delivering the sumfnons to Frederick Cilinnett instead of to eland Ginnett ; ,beat that did net make defendant liable, neither was IS sufficient to bring Clawl trinnett to that court. He should amend the proceedings and make Claud Ginlett the defendant in the action, there- fore the jury would be discharged, and an order made for . defendant's costs.

Weverantorole v. A 911TON-lINDER•LYNB (A TEAus).— The above teams met for the first time at Ashton-under- Lyne on Saturday. Whittle kicked off, the ball being re- turned to touch at mid-field. From the line out Gilbert got hold and passed to Belehaw, the latter running well into the borne team'e quarters. The Ashton forwards, headed by Tunnicliffe, retaliated with a good dribble, and removed play to the visitors' 25, when from a scrimmage they rushed the ball over into touch in goal. Gilbert dropped out, and the ball being well returned a scrimmage was formed on the Warrington line. Gilbert by a run and kick removed play to mid-field, and Whittle by a dribble took the ball to the home team's 25. Astiton. however, again rushed it back to the Warringtonians. Boardman now got hold, and ran tbe ball back to mid-field. From a scrimmage Leach picked up and took his drop at goal unsuccessfully, the ball going dead. This brought about half time, the scores being Ash- ton two minors, Warrington nil. Yegall kicked off, and from a pass by Bedford to Morris the latter put in a good run, but was finely collared by Acton. The visitors for- wards now broke away, but Morris picking up smartly made: a dash for the visitors line, and was only 'knocked into touch when looking dangerous. From the scrimer age fol. lowing Warrington were forced to tough down. On drop- ping out Boardman put its a good run to centre. The ball was, however, soon returned to the visitors 25. The Warrington forwards, by a com- bined dribble, took the ball nearly the whole length of the field, forcing Lowndes to kick it dead, Warrington thus scoring their first point. From the drop oat Belskaw failed to return, rind after some loose play at centre Acton obtained posaession and ran well to the home quarters and Warrington rushed over, the ball going dead. On dropping out Acton put in another good run, and the home team were again forced to touch down. Shortly after "nu side" was called seven minutes Were time on account of the darkness, the play then being well in the home 25. lbe game thus resulted in a draw—three minors each. War- rington in the second half had by far the test of the game, and for the last quarter of an hour penned the home team on their line. For Aslit it Morris. Redford, and Yoza.ll, back, and Leach, Tunnicliffe, and Walsh, forward, were the best. Warrington played a very good game all round, and it would be unfair to specially mention any-player. TfIE UPLOSIVES ACT. ,
mosEcunoNs AT St HELENS.
A singular aeries of promotions under the ExploAivea Act, 1875, were heard at the Si. Helens Town Hall, on Mon- day, before Mr. Win. Pilkington, Dr. E. P . Xwyford, and Alderman J. Harriaon.

In the first case Rttert 011erton, a grocer at Parr Hill, Rainfoed, was summoned for keeping 27Ibp. of gunpow,ler and 33Ibs. of blasting powder in an unauthorised place.— Superintendent Jphnston stated that the defendant formerly held a license to Veep sth be. of powder, but tbd license ex- pired on the 13th Juiy last. He had not since renewed it, and on Inspector Whittaker visiting the place be fonnd 601bs. of powder stored therein.—The defendant urged that it was through an oversight that the license had not been renewed.—The magistrates remarked that they would hear the whore; of the cases before giving a.decislon. • James Rougbley, grow, Bushy-lane, &Word,' was 'charged with keeping 301bs. of powder In an unatitlniftd place, on the 13•11 N9Tettl'Yl —lf waif statEd tb.,t &fen. dant's forma llcase expired in May LA Inspector nbit-, taker visited the place, and found 3011 as. of powder on the 11th Nevember.—la reply to Mr. J.O Swift, of Bs. firlens, who defended, .Inspector Whiitaker stated that the defen- dant had informed him be Would have renewed his license, only he was under the impression that it would be sufficient if it was renewed any time each year. Renewals of gun- powder licensee only cost le per year.—Mr. Swift explained that this latter statement was the fact, and said that his client had foolishly believed it would be legal to take oat his renewal at any time. _ _

Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., colliery proprietors, gale dock, were summoned for keeping 245 blasting cartridges in an unauthorised place at Havannah Colliery, on the lOch November.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the firm, who were represented by Mr. Beilby.—Superintendent Johnston ex- plained that the defendants were formerly registered to keep 4,0001b5.,0f powder in a store at the Havasnah but when the store was inspected by Colonel Ford a new magazine was built. The license expired on the 2213 Sep- tember last—lnspector Whittaker deposed that in the old magazine be found 100Ibs. of gunpowder, and in another place 2451b5. of powder, whereas the place was only regis- tered to hold 200Ihs. of poirder. In the store be found I,ooolbs. of pewder.—Mr. Swift said the defen- dants were licensed to hold 4,0001b5. of powder, and it WAS only by an oversight that the license had been allowed to lapse. There had been no intention to set the law at defi- ance or to break it. Messrs. Bronsilow, Foster, and Co., of the 'Ashton's Green Colliery (for whom Mr. J. f. Elliott appeared), were sum- moned for storing 75Ibs of tonite, a substance of the nature of dynamite, in a place only registered for the storage of gunpowder. The defendants were registered to store I,ooolbs of gunpowder, but when Inspector Whittaker visited their store be found 751bs of tonite. A special license wee re- quired for the storage of the latter substance.—Mr. Elliott said his employers had unwittingly allowed a breach of the Act. They had a license for gunpowder and it was thought that it covered other explosives, but the tonite had since been removed.

Robert Goldthorpe Brook, ironmonger, Raven-street, St. Helene, was summoned for a breach of the Explosives Act by tailing to affix a notice to the door of his powder store warning persons of their danger. Inspector Whittaker said be visited the defendant's store at ktavenhead, and there was no notice on tbe door warning trespassers.—Mr. Swift bald notices had been regularly posted on the door, but they were tore down.—lnspector Whittaker (in reply to Mr. saift; admitted that there were several tacks In the door, and there were pieces of paper attached.—Mr. Swift submit- ted that no offence bad been committed, end produced a printed copy of a notice which be said bad been affixed to the door.—Job e Peers deposed that he had seen a notice poated on the door, and John Ellison, an apprentice em- ployed by Mr. Brook, said he frequently posted notices on the door, but they were pulled down.

The next case was one in which John Billinge, grocer. Park-road, St. Helens, was summoned for keeping 12Ibs of blastieg cartridges in an unregistered pi see. Defendant Pleaded guilty.--Superintendent Johnston stated that de- fendant's license expired on the 30th May last.—Defend- ant : Surely you don't think we are going to turn rogues for a shilling: I think the Act is decidedly wrong. (Lanzhter.)—Tbe Chairman said they had to obey the law, and tse Bench wished to know if he had any excuse to offer or not taking out a I icsnse after the 30th of May.—Defend- ant maid those who had licenees never received any notice when they expired and he thought the law was wrong in that respect. He admitted there was a degree of careless- ness about it as well.

Benjamin Tickle, a grocer at 11. Sutton-road, was sum- mon,d for keeping 931bs. of powder without a licence.— Inspector Whittaker said the defendant was formerly licensed to store 501bs. of powder, but he had allowed hia licence to lapse. When he visited the place he found 931bs. of powder.—Defendant said he was not aware that the licence had run out, and in explan4tion of having too much on his premises, said he was sold out of powder and he gave an order fer 5011)4, Owing to its delay in coming he purchased another 501 Is. is order to supply a custneper, and on the day following his order of 50Ibs. was received. Messrs. B. B. Glover asd Company, of the Phcenix Col- liery, Ravenhead, Was summoned for storing a greater quantity of punpowder that that for which they held a licence.—Mr. Swift, who appeared for the defendants, said they pleaded guilty.—lnspector Whittaker deposed that he visited the defandants' colliery, and in the store which was licensed to bold 300Ibn. he found 400ibs. of gunpowder.— For the defence, Mr. Swift said the defendants had pro- perly renewed their licence. They were at present engaged in sinking a pit a: Sutton, and used 200Ihs. weight of pow- der every week. The pit was, however, flooded with water early iu November, the blasting operations being entirely stopped therei,y for sometime. They al lowrd their usual weekly quantity of gunpowder to be taken int. the store, but unfortunately they were unable to stop the flooding. Thy would not have bad the excessive quantity if it had not been for the stoppage of the work. The magistrates retired to consider the eases, and were absent for ten minutes —On their return the Chairman said the Bencb bad decided to floe 011erton £1 and costs, £1 12s; Rouehley 104 and costs, £l. 2s ; Messrs Richard Evans and Company Li and costs, £1 11; Bromilow, Foster, and Compmy £1 and costs, II 11.1 ; John Billings 104 and costa. Li is: Benjamin Tickle £1 and costs, £1 us ; Messrs. Ol;ever and Company £1 and costa, El Ile; cad the case against Robert bloldtborpe Brook would be dis- missed.

EAHLINTOWN GOOD TEMPLMIS AT ASHTON. —Accord- ing to arrangements previously made, about 30 members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars visited Ashton on Monday night, and gave an entertainment in the Congregational schoolroom, under the auspices of the Band Of Hope Society. The chair was occupied by the Rev. 11.-nry Wilson, pastor, wile, after the singing of a hymn, gave an addreas on the objocts of that entertainment and alluded to the great importance of temperance work. A choir, under tie leadership of Brother George Clarke, then sang the melody " Wondroos love." after which Sister Lackland recited " Duty before pleasure,' and the quar- tette " Summer rain " was sung Icy Sisters Mrs and S. J. Walker and tiros J. Walker and G. Clarke. Sister M Whittv nest sang lam lonely sinCe my mother died." and Brother John Wathotton was deservedly encored for the recitation " While the Sahliath bells were ringing." He responded with " The gambler's wife." Brother J. Bar- nard next read " The good angels," which was followed by the melody "Whiter than anew" by the choir A recita- tion "The compensation cry" was given by Broth, r George Clarke, and Sisters Emily and Jane Clarke sang the dutet "Must I go, and empty handed? " Sister Mrs E. Whit Y rang "Crouching 'neath Vie arch," and the choir gave " stand by until the moro:ng." Brother George E. Warbui-- ton recited "Ntliti's Christmas box" and OD being re- called he recited 'The little wanderer." " Hark, I hear era angel sing " was sung by Sister C. Jackson, and the entertainment concluded with a cordial vote of thanks paid to the Earlesrown friends for their entertainment, and the visitors were afterwards entertained to enjoyable. supper.

SNOWSTORM —Accounts from Scotland report a continua- tion of the snowstorm in the north, with a block of high- roads and railways and much consequent discomfort to travelkrs. Two of the Caithness ballot boxes are delayed en route, owing to the ob.truction of the roads. One of the polling officers was plodding through the snow with his ballot boxes on Wednesday for live hours. THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 12 1885 CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c. "The Graphic Christmas Number" preserves the high reputation it has attained. There is a double coloured premeetation plate—" Down" and "Up ; " the one representing a sweet little girl on a sick bed, and another as she is when she it "up "again. The pictures, after the originals by W. L. Thomas, are capital pieces of work, the dog figuring finely in both. But dog life is bbet pourtrayed in the adven- tures of "Pincher" from drawings by C. Burton Barber. " Curmudgeon's Christmas" is alike amus- ing in text and illustrations, the latter being in Mr. R. Caldeeott'a best style. Other coloured pictuies are "Rehearsing for the Pantomime," "A Raid on the Dessert," "United Service," and " Tired Out," and there are numerous engravings. In the way of story, the great feature is " The History of a week," by Mee. L. B. Walford. The title-page is a novelty ; it represents little ones engaged in petting on A screen the pictures to be found within the Christ- mas number. The presentation plate with the Christmas namber of the " Illustrated London News " is a reproduction of Sir J. E. famous picture of "The north- west passake." is splendidly executed, and, suit- ably framed,. tt will adorn many a wall curing the (riming year. Another special feature is a pair of fine engravings on superior paper—one of Long- fellow's ''Priscilla," from a drawing by Florence Grovier, and the other "Roses" (two rose maidens), from a drawing by M. Walker. " Welshem Grange; a Real Ghost Story," drawn and written by E. Morant COX, is in every way excellent. The number is strong in short stories; Mr. James Payne contributes " Mr. Blodger's Apology ; " Mr. B. L. Farjeon, "A Bright Ending ; " and Mr. Compton Reads, "The Double Iris." The latter, however, is scarcely worthy of Mr. Reeds, the story turninr as it does on a hinge which has been too much used. There are other tales and eke:chem, with a wealth of illnetrakion of the very highest "The Magazine of Art" for December is especially interesting for its graphic reproduction of notable portraits of such celebreties as ,Prinee Bismarck, Pope Leo lII', and Franz Liszt. The coloured frontispiece is very brilliant. In " Artists' Homes" we have an account (Migrated) of Mr. Harry Fermis and his surreundinga at Montclair, New Jereey. "A Polish Village in November" is from a charming picture by A. Wierasz Kowalieki ; while Summer, from the picture by Sichel, is equally charming. • Among the interesting articles we have "The Royal Academy's instrument and how they got it," " Some Japanese Painters," 4. The rpper Medway," and "The Romance of Arts" Sure and Swift " is the title of the Christmas number of ' The Quiver." It has a very pretty col- oured frontispiece, and a number of striking engrav- ings. There is music and veree, and half a dozen ex- cellent complete stories. " Winter Blossoms " is issued as the annual of " Little Folk,' The Chrittmat decoration of an old clock makes a ~.,very pretty frontispiece, by Alice • Havers, and when we add that there are other trationa by Harry Furness, Palmer Cox, W. Hather- ell, &c., it will be sufficient to suggest that the num- ber must be a good one. " Cassell's Illustrated Almanac" is always wel- • corned as a wonderful sixpennyworth. The issue for 1856 is in no respect inferior to its predecessors. To • may nothing a the large amount of carefully prepared , information which it contains, it is worth the price charged as a picture-book for the children. - Messrs. Cassell announce that they will shortly 1. begin the weekly pnblitettion of a series of Three- penny imprints of good literature. Each velume, which will be Complete in itself, will Contain abou Li fee pages, emall.Eve, printed in clear readable type, , I alai it is pretniteal that the series, which is to be . entitlea Caeiell's national Library," shall represent , all periods and forms of thought, and shall include , the records of history, biography, religion, philoso• • phy, di-covery, enterprise, natural science, natural , history, art, and political economy, as well as plays, ; poems, and tales, and whatever else may be worth hating remembrance. The publishers have secured the services of Professor Henry Morley as editor of the new library. ' •' The Season " for December, in addition to the , usual coloured fashion plates, and numerous engray. ling; and patterns, has a gratuitous Christmas supple I enent, consisting of Flower Children—a novelty in eliesigns for children's fancy Costumes for Christmas' parties. The designs are printed in sepia, and col- oured by hand. There is also a &allele pare fine-art , engraving of Christmas in St. Mark's Cathedral, Venice. "Le Monitear de la Mode" has also made special provieien for the festive season with costumes • for fancy dress balls, Menus for Christmas Dinners, 'ko. " Myries Journal" is exceedingly strong, the ' December number being double. The presentation ' picture, " Once upon a Time," is very pretty indeed, and is well worthy of a frame. We have also to ' hand " Myra's Threepenny Journal" for December. CHRISTXLS CARDS, &D.— "Art is long," but it is everywhere having its effect, and nowhere more „ markedly than in the production of Christmas cards. , 'lettere. Hildesheimer and Faulkner, London, who are , at the head of the trade in fine-art Christmas cards, ' spend large sums of money every year in prizes for , the best designs; and the result is that we have "linked sweetness long drawn out." Glancing through an assorted parcel from this firm, we cannot but marvel at their beauty. The designs are very 'varied and very charming ; they are brilliant and yet refined; striking and delicate, and exquisite as to finish. Mr. Frank Feller's designs representing horse•guard, life-guard, dragoon and lancer, stand in the front rank, each being a picture in itself. Mr. Fred Blues cleverly shows what can be done with naked trees and setting suns. Alice Havers, the de- signer of the elegant show card, and Jane M. Deely are both delightful in revealing the charms of children. Mr. Albert Bowers makes one fall in love with a farm-yard in winter, while Linnie Watt reminds us of summer with her merry children on the sea shore. The sea is also well represented by Mr. Percy Robertson's sepia sketches; and we have the "bonnie birds " by Alice West, Flowers and birds are wonderfully depicted by Mr. Ernest Wilson, and Mr. C. G. Noakes, while Mr. B. D. Sigmund shows himself at horns with scenery of every kind. ' The landscapes and seaecapee of F. C. and A. Price are ' exceedingly suggesdve, and will not fail to.attract the eye of the student of nature and of art. Mr. W. J. Hodgson furnishes some sketches which are amus- ing without being coarse; and the same may be said ,of Mr. Frank Feller's attitudinising niggers. Those who want "the o irrect card need not go beyond , those supplied by Meesrs. Hildesheimer and Faulkner; if they go farther they will be likely to fare worse. The same firm also ieeue children's illustrated books, and we willingly testify that they are marvels or beauty. "The White Swans" and other tales by Hans Anderson is illnetrated by Alice Havers ; while " Throuirh the Meadows," a book of poems by Fred E. Weatbley, is adorned with coloured illustrations by Mr. E. Edwards, and monotintm by John C Staples. I Both works are extraordinary of their kind ; they are , a long way ahead of anything we have previously seen. They are really so charming that it seems a pity to touch them.

_ _ OAS AND WATBR COMMITTEE :—INCRBASB OF SALADS/. To the Gas and Water Cetntnittee Mr. Carr reported : " Sulphate of Ammonia Plant—This apparatus is now t fairly at work, and about 13 tons of grey sulphate of good quality has been made. Every trace of ammonia is taken out of the liquor. We are able to make as good a quality of sulphate flout common vitriol as from pure ; the price of the former being less than half that of the letter. The specification required that the plant should be capable of distilling 7 tons of 10-cz_ liquor per diem, but 1 find that we could, if necessary, distil a much greater quantity. A small parcel of the sulphate has been purchased by Messrs. Ceskell, Deakin, and Co., and I have since been informed I Iby them that it tested over 24 per cent, of ammonia. The ' I manufacture of sulphate if anamonit beiag subject to the regulations of the .sekali Act; both local and district inspec- tors have examined the apparAtas and expressed themselves highly satisfied with th'e arrangements for the ahserption of the noxious gases evolved in the process."— The mean rainfall fur the month WAS 2532 inches. The illuminating power of the gas had averaged 17-02 candlee. It was recommended that Mr. Carr's salary be increased £5O per annum in consideration of bis extra duties in connection I with the sulphate of ammonia manufacture. I Mr. Gaskell, in moving the adoption of the minutes, re- ferred to the extremely satisfactory condition of the sul- phate-of ammonia manufacture, and the committee thought that Mr. Carr deserved Some addition to nis salary M conse- quence of the extra labour thet would be entailed upon him. The quantity of gas they were making was iecreasing at the rate of rather over 12 per cent, per annum, and the water. pumped had increased at the rate of 20 per cent, per annum. By the meamfActure of sulphate of ammonia the committee expected to save At leAst £1 000 per anriwn, so that they ooutd well afford to pay Mr Carr an increased sultry. He moved in conclusion that the tender of the Gas Puritication Company to supply oxide of iron free of cast, the oxide tte be returned f.o.r. without any guarantee as to the per cep- tags of sulphur, be accepted. Mr. Sadler eecouded the motions, which were adopted neat con.

To this committee the medical officer that during Novemb thee rere 100 births and 29 deaths, being at the rate of 44.44 and 1288 per 1,000 respectively. Dr.—Olieeffe reported that the property in question was in Anne-street, and, he believed, was in existence before the formation of the Local Board. THE NOTIFICATION OF INFECTIOUS DISEASES. In accordance with notice he gave at the last meeting, Dr. O'Bet-ffe moved that the resolution to pay 2s 61 to the medical Men for each case of infectious disease they reported be rescinded. The medical men, he said, refused to report all cases, but at the same time promised to dive every aid to to the Authority in stamping out infectious disease. They did not appear to be very solicitous about the half-crown. Mr. Sadler seconded the motion, which was carried. THE TOWN BALL QUESTION: TREE LIBRARY

The following letter was read :- "Marsh alkali to ors, Widnes, December 7th, 1885. , Chairman of the Widnes Local Rood. Dear sir,—The I erection of buildings for public offices and town hall being one of the subjects for discussion at your next meeting, permit me to euggest that.this is a favourable time for your Board to take into consideration the question of setting apart a portion of the building for reading-room and library. I venture to urge upon the Board the necessity of providing such an institution in Widnes, where there is nothing of interest to occupy the working-men during their leisure time. I feel sure the ratepayers will sup ion your Board in carrying out a scheme so much calculated to promote the welfare and true interest of the people. A visit to the neighbouring towns of St. Helens, Runcorn, Liverpool, &c, will convince anyone of the importance of such a place. In Liverpool, now that trade is so bad, the reading-room is crowded day and night mostly by working people. If we wish to retain t'ee better class of men as residents we must make the town as attractive as poesible and offer all the advantages we can.—Yours truly, R. H. Davtas. Don't let Runcorn have all the good things" Dr. O'Keeffe argued as on the last occasion that at least £2OO would be derived from the Town Hall in Widnes, and that seven-eights of a penny in the £ would cover the re- mainder of the expense. He considerid that the Town Hall would be no loss whatever to the ratepayers. a, r. Davies put the matter very strongly indeed in his letter, and he was very glad that a gentleman who lived out of the township should rake such a deep Biterest in the poor fel- lows who were obliged to reside in it. It would be very well if other gentlemen who resided outside would take a similar interest and make provision for a reading-room. The architects had made ample provisions for a reading - room and library in the complete plan for the Town Hall and public (aces, and these would be one of the greatest boons the town could have. There were no places of interest or amusement for the people at Widnes except the the public- houses, and there was nothing elevating or moral about those. There was nothing that would tend to elevate the moral tone of the town more than a reading-room and a library, and if, as Mr. Chamberlain said, they were to have free education, he asked what good would it be to the people unless they had a library and reading-room. People improved themselves a thousand times more by private study after they left school, but in Widnes there was not the slightest inducement to self study. • Ile referred to the envier advantages possessed by towns the neighbour- hood, and nr.tved that the entire echeine for town h5ll and public office tik completed. Br. Forster seconded. •

Mr. Ileyes thought this was tha most favourable time for carrying Oat the undertakinz. Materials and labour were cheap. Mr. Handley said on tne question of finance he agreed with Mr Allan that £lO,OOO would mean an annual pay- ment of £578 se. They might calculate upon having an income from letting the hall at £2OO a year. At Runcorn the public hall brought in a clear income of £lOO a year. ' Considering that there were several other rooms in that town that were let for public entertainments, he thought that in Widnes, which WAS twice the size, and the fact that the town hall would be the only imitable room, they might reasonably calculate upon a revenue •f £2OO A year. Mr. Gaekell said Mr. Handley had spoken of the large assessments although the objEctiou might come from them. Mow, be did not anticipete that it was from them that any objection raised would come. It was the email assess- ments which would have great difficulty in making both ends niter, and who looked at a shilling before thew would part with it, who would be the most likely to object. He thought before they went into the whole scheme it would be well to ascertain the wishes of the ratepayers generally. He therefore suggested that • public rneeritig of ratepayers should be called. Marshal Caatilline, among other singular ides, had a mania for questioning his officers about their familiee, his invariable rude of Interrogation being, "Whit IS Your father's profession your mother's, and your sister's?" This stereotyped repetition became at last so wearisome that some of his young sabalterns agreed on the following reply, to be given by cook in turn—" My father is a shoemaker, my mother a laundress, and my sister very flighty." On the ensuing Sunday, after the Renal military parade, the marshal, who had reoeived the same answer to his questions , from three officers, turned to the fourth, and reeentmenced, in his amestemed strain, "What is your father's proles- elan ?" "He is a shoemaker." "And your mother's?' "She is a laundress." "That will do," interrupted the chief, "I know the reet; your sister is very flighty; and you will consider yourself confined to barraeks until she behaves better."

Twit ANGLO-INDIAN "ML"—A living writer says of dress :—"Don't wear apparel with decided detours or with pronotanoed patterns." The Anglo-Indian "masher," however, scorns this wholesome and trite advice, and de- votes all his energy to routing out and securing the "loudest " and the most pronounced patterns for the snits that adorn his manly form. Apropos of such garments the following genuine story is worth repeating :---The sone is laid in the reading-room of a club in India. Enter a •• masher" eonselous of the uniqueness of the pattern of his new snit, who is immediately congratulated by a brother "masher" on the chaste pattern. The first "masher," highly pleased., eonfidingly reveals that he invented the pattern, and proudly adds that he does not think that there is another like it in the world, to which the other cor- dially assents. At this point an elderly gentleman, who ap till then had apparently been engrossed in the newspaper, outs in with "I beg your pardon; I have often seen that pattern before." " Where?" incredulously asked the "mashers." "In Colney Hatch. All the dangerous lunatic's who have maltreated their keepers are clothed in that pattern of suit, in order to distinguish them from the more quietly-behaved members of the institution." Tablets& !

It is well known that the Americans are a very practical people, even in their religion. One of them has just in- vented a berglar-proof safe which, when tampered with, suddenly extends a powerful pair of tongs or grippers, which seize the malefactor and hold him in a arm embrace. There is nothing extraordinarily new is all this, bet there M something farther. Nearly always Wee that are likely te be viesited by burglars are in buildings unoccupied durieg the night, and it is only the next morning that the cap- tured robber is carefully released from the trap to be duly imprisoned. This is, of °ours., time lost, whieh the religions inventor desires to utilise. He has therefore had prepared by an eloquent preacher a very long and remarkably forcible sermon, in which the rights of property, the dis- grace of stealing, and the dangers attendant on it, both in this world and the next, are set forth in the most touching language. The sermon, stored in a phonograph, is started lat the earns moment 'that the pincers operate, and the homily is rolled out in the ears of the " paint." The I monotonous nasal tone peculiar to the phonograph renders the illusion perfect; the unfortunate robber believes he hears the preacher himself, and in the morning, when the police arrive, they find him thoroughly:subdued and repen- i amt.

div.head: JOB DYSON'S VOTE.
div.p: JOB DYSON'S VOTE.
By Bloc Bantruranr.

Job Dyson had never v-o-ied-b-efo7e7either for municipal candidates nor parliamentary; and the process of tenderiag a vote wan, now that he had come into a qualification by removing from a country village to Manchester, quite a novelty to hint. He had always understood that the ballot meant secrecy; and he was determined to uphold the in- tegrity of the system—no one should have the least inkling of the way be voted. He would not even satisfy his neigh- bours as to whether he was a Tory, or a Radical, but kept them in a state of nervous uncertainty as to what he was likely to do on the day of election, which was drawing near. A municipal contest was the event, when Job would be called upon to discharge a duty, and decide which of two candidates he would support. Hie vote would 'make a difference ef two in the counting, and as it was expected that the race would be close running, both parties were anxious that he should be got at. He had been canvassed until no one would venture near big door, for fear of its being slammed in his face. To each question, "Who did he intend voting for?' the invariable answer was, with a few strong words added towards the int— i•l vote by ballot, I do; an' if thean doeeno' get away fro this der I'll help thee wi' my foot." Consequently the canvasser's lantern was seen on several occasions to shoot like a meteor from the door, a precipitate retreat, that was a warning to others. But the polling day came, and armed with his newly- I acquired authority, Job Dyson went to record his vote. There was no lack of people, he found when he reached the polling place, who were desirous of 1" coaching him. but to each of these he would observe—" I vote by ballot!' "But what is your number ?" demanded an individual more officious than the rest; and seeing that our friend was bewildered with the array of 'rithmetic before him. "If theau thinks theatert gooin to get that canto' me theau'll ha' to bore holes into me, an' get it taut by drops; so thee mind thy own bizness, and thean shall have a new dicky." And Job gripped the card he held in his hand as though he meant to strangle it. " I clar'say thean thowt I're a new cacht on, ut hadao' getten th' brid-lime off my wings; but theau'll find I'm as owd a brid as thee." A policeman, hearing what was going on, stepped up to our friend, and asked him what was his number. • "What, art' therm moddlin', too?' said Job, indignantly; "1 thowt thy wtrk wur thief catchin', an' no' tryin' to catch sich like as me. But I con tell thee what, Mestker Bobby, if thean carries thy number on thy collar, so ut everybody con see it, I carry mine wheere it's safe." "Well, but which booth do you vote in ?" demanded the man in blue. . .

"I'm noane partikilar which o' theeee boosee I goo into. They're mooestly of a pattern for owt I set. I'll tak th' fast, and in Job went. "What Is your name ?" demanded the presiding officer of our "free and enlightened" fellow-citizen. • "Job Dyson," wag the answer "Dyson Job," said the chairman, running his finger-down the list before him. "Not here." -
"I said Job Dyson, no' Dyeo-n— Job," insisted the applicant for municipal privileges.

The presiding offieer could not dnd the name in his list; and Job still refused to show his voting card. It was not until he reached the last booth that his name could be found, and the discovery was hailed with expressions of satisfaction by the bewildered voter. Job entered the hex, and with an allusion to Puowb. and Judy that was just audible, pulled himself together for work. It wee sometime before he could fairly reconcile himself as to what wee his duty; but after sucking the pen- cil as if it had been a stick of candy, he Tel:Awed to mark his paper. Folding the document as he had been taught to do, he dropped it in the nick, and then looked eider the table, as though he thought the ballot box was a kind of mill for grinding up votes, and passed them in a powdered state to some place below. "I'Te made a mesa eV that job," he exclaimed, staring at the presiding officerss if jest awakening out of a stupid dream. "I've cone an' Toted for th' wrong mon. SHIPWRECKS AND LOS 3 OF I INK AND PROPERTY.—The steamer Delta has arrived at Halifax from the wreck of the Liverpool steamer Brooklyn. The Delta had some salved cargo from the Broolvn, as well as 35 head of cattle and 17 sheep. The vessel Dufferin was by the wreck when the Delta left, and was half full of the salved cargo. The Brooklyn herself was then breaking up. The ship Dun- , drenuan, ef Liverpool (Captain 111‘Noah), arrived in Penarth ' Boads with a cargo of grain from Calcutta on Tuesday ' evening. The captain reports thaton November 24th, when R little te the 130,0 of Ow Weltern Islands, the Shin en. I Countered a terrific gala. About half-past ten o'clock in the morning she was running before it at the rate of eleven knots. Some of the crew were engaged bracing the fore. yards forward, when she shipped two or three seas in succes- sion, which filled the decks, washing five of the seaman and an apprentice overboard. Ropes were thrown to them, but of no avail. No boat could have lived in such a sea, and it wee impossible to bring the ship to the wind, It. Lloyd, 'A.B.. wan wash,cl overboard, and the next wave washed him on board again.where he was picked up very seriously bruised.l On Sunday the steamer Hayle, of Aberde, n, which left that port for Sunderland on Saturday night, put into Arbroath, with her fotehold full of water, having been in collision with an unknown vessel about It 3 miles east of the Bell Rock Lighthouse early on Sunday morning. The unknown vessel was struok amidships, and sank almost Immediately. A boat was lowered from the Hayle, but none of the crew of the other vessel could be seen, and it is feared they all perished. Fourteen sailing vessels have been stranded by a hurricane at Aspinwall, Panama. All the steamers there put to sea when the storm was seen approaching. The schooners Grace and William and Jane, which left Scar- borough for Hartlepool, a six hours' voyage, have not since been heard of.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THITBSD.A.Y.

The general election is now practically over, and the result justifies the sanguine view' which, with almost universal exception, has from the first been taken in this correspondence. I admit that I was not prepared for the full effect of the Irish vote in the boroughs, nor was it possible for an honest Liberal to anticipate that six seats would be wan- tonly handed over to the Conservatives owing to the personal ambition and reckless selfishness of a few men. My faith was pinned upon the counties, and it has been abundantly justified. A majority of 84, which will probably be increased by twp or three when the result of the remaining six elections is made known, is a national vote of confidence in a statesman rarely excelled. This is a matter in which the Irish vote has no moral weight. With cynical frankness its position in the market is openly avowed. Mr. Parnell has 86 votes at his command, and he makes no scruple in declaring that he will sell them to the highest bidder. This was known beforehand, and its effects were dis- counted. Lord Salisbury appealed to Great Britain to decide between him and My. Gladstone, and the decision is emphatic and unmistakeable. I Satiated with the interest hourly culminating in Ithe General Election, the public now turn with re- vived eagerness to ask what will follow? Amid much that is conjectural one thing appears certain. Lord Salisbury will not go till he is carried out. Mr. Disraeli, defeated in 1880 by a majority of English votes little more than that which has now condemned Lord Salisbury, immediately retired from office as Mr. Gladstone in similar circum- stances had done in 1874: But, with all their rever- ence for the departed leader, Conservative office- holders of to-day scout his example and linger on for another morth of pay and power. Since they unexpectedly came into office in July last they have made an exceedingly good thing of their oppor- tunity. There have been peerages, places, pensions, and a picnic for Sir Hy. Wolff. No one can tell what a day may bring forth. Judges and bishops have, on the average, reached an age that makes a man peculiarly liable to sudden cutting off, and all the 'men who would like to be bishops or hope to be judges are concerned in Lord Salisbury's holding in, his hands till the very last moment the disposi- tion of patronage. Therefore Lord Salisbury, re- gardless of precedent and careless of the precepts of the constitution, declines to accept his pereMp- tory dismissid and stay% in office. Of course, this kind of thing cannot last long. Parliament will meet on the 12th of January, and it is within the bounds of possibility that there- upon the Government may be turned out. Accord- ing to present appearances, however, they will be permitted another month's official existence. The proceedings at the opening of Parliament will be ,purely formal. There will be the Speaker to select, but that does not promise to be an exciting affair. Had the Liberal 'majority been less, and had Sir Matthew White Ridley succeeded in keeping his seat, the' Conservatives would have put him up in opposition to Mr. Peel. In this they would have had the enthusiastic support of the Parnellites, who hate Mr. Peel even more than they did Sir Hemy Brand, and for the reason that he has proved an abler and more commanding president. Even apart from this personal consideration, it wouldsuit the Parnellite game admirably to have public business at the beginning of a new Parliament embarrassed by the appointment of a new Speaker, who however able he might be would not at the outset possess that authority or knowledge essen- tial to the due guidance of a newly constituted assembly. These are considerations which have no 'weight with the Constitutional party. They were quite prepared to put a slight upon Mr. Peel, the ablest Speaker of modern times, and throw the machinery of public business into confusion in order to gratify partisan feeling. Happily they are impotent in this respect,. and Mr. Peel will return to the chair he has filled with dignity. The House will meet again early in February, and then will commence the tug of war. In the usual course an Address in reply to tlk Speech from the Throne will be moved, and thereupon issue will be joined in the triangular duel. Either Mr. Gladstone or Mr. Parnell may move an amendment, and a cri- tical division may take place. I am disposed to think that a still further term of grace will be secured by the Ministry. The one questions of the session will be 'lreland. But Lord Salisbury will not fail to see the necessity of placing in the fore- front of his programme a promise to deal with local government in the sister country. Upon the Ad- dress he is not bound to describe the clauses of a bill not yet introduced, and it would be difficult for either Mr. Gladstone or Mr. Parnell to turn the Premier out on a bill they have not seen. I think matters will drift on till the Government bill is laid before the House, when storms will burst forth from all quarters of the political heavens. Whigs, Radi- cals, Liberals, Conservatives, Tories, and Irish Orangemen, each and all bold strong views upon the Irish questimi, and will not fail to express .them. , The Government will almost certainly come to grief on the bill, A con- tingency for which I believe Lord Salisbury is well prepared. It is impossible for him without break- ing up his own party and coming into contact with the Lords to propose a measure that would satisfy the aspirations of Mr. Parnell. But he must at least affect to deal with the subject. What he will do will be to bring in a moderate bill which will not offend the Sensibilities of his Irish folliwers, and which may gain the approval of moderate Liberals and the sanction of the House of Lords. If he car- ries it, well and good. If the more likely result fol- lows of a defeat of the Ministry, he will at once appeal to the country with a cry against the Irish and the Radicals, and' in March next we may be 11 once more in the throes of a general election. The elections have been followed with intense in- , terest, and have supplied openings for ready con- versation ind means by which many new hats and golden sovereigns have been transferred. But it has been a very bad thing for trade, and there are many to sing praises now it is over. There were times when a general election meant the dispensa- tion of vast sums of'money. Sir George Elliot, who has, owing to the Liberal reaction in the north,' followed his son into obscurity, knows something of this. Ile spent a fortune in fighting North Dur- ham in 1868, and another in the struggle of 1874. For this Mr. Disraeli gave him a baronetcy ; but" it was dearly purchased. Now things are altogether different. The sum spent upon the election just closed is not a tythe of that spent upon the election of 1874: My friend, whom I mentioned the other day, going to the scene of electoral conflict in a third-class carriage, indicates the straits'to which members are now put to bring their expenses within the statutory sum. This Spartan economy has told upon the Liberals in more ways than one. The pro- hibition of hiring carriages for the convenience of voters seriously hampered them in some counties. The kind of people who used to grow fat on the lavish expenditure of the old style of candidate bitterly resented the enforced economy of the present election, and vented their spite upon the represen- tative of the party that brought it about. This feeling is believed to have influenced the result of the polling in many constituencies. Now the elec- tions, so unsatisfactory from a trade.man's point of view, are happily over, and we may look for the full I development of the improvement in trade, of which so much is said and written.

Everyone has been riu-r-P-ii.sed and/delighted with Lord Tennyson's new book. It seemed that when the poet became a peer he had lost the priceless gift which no Sovereign could bestow. Within the last few years he has written much pitiful stuff, which without his name would not obtain admis- sion to the poet's corner of a local newspaper. Now he has amazed the world by presenting it with a Christmas box in the shape of a book of poems which in their way equal the best efforts of his best days. "Tiresias," it is true, was written many years ago. But that 'does not explain everything. Some of the poems, notably that in the Irish dia- lect entitled "To-morrow," has been recently written. Those jealous for the fame of Tennyson, and.grateful for all the delight he has given them in time past, will hope that these may be his last offerings. He cannot do better, and alas! has in recent years done much worse.

It is Curious to note how phrases uttered by great men which happened to strike the ear of the public are misquoted. There is, for example, Mr. Disraeli's famous reply to Lord Robert Montagu when in the early days of the session of the new Parliament the noble lord inconveniently quoted One remarks made by Mr. Disraeli before the elections to his constituents at Buckingham with respect to Ire- land. Lord Robert wanted to know whether now Mr. Disraeli was in power he intended to carry out the recommendations he had then pressed upon the Liberal Government. Everyone will be prepared to swear that what Mr. Disraeli ,Said was "A great deal has happened since then.' His actual words were "It is some time since the observations re- ferred to were made, and a good deal has happened in the interval." Still more deeply rooted is the belief that Mr. Carlyle once said that England was

Sir,—A* an occ.tsional visitor at our Borough Police Court. I have often noticed the cenflicting evidence given before the magistrates by the various witnesses concerned in a case. The evidence in some summons cases, principally priv.l quvriih, is of so contradictory a character as 'to lrlve no doubt that perjury is being committed, but by which side it is imuossiole to tell. Thus the justices are often nlaced in a difficulty, and are really compelled to dis- miss-the summons. It would, perhaps, he hard to find a remedy for the vast amount of perversion of truth going in, Init I would suggest that a strict watch be kept, and that if perjury could he proved, proceedings should at once be Vikeu. It totght hAve a deterrent bffect.—Yourp.,iro . TRUTH.

MEASURES BEFORE MEN. Sir,—The long letter of Mr. A. Rathbone, which ap- peared in your. last week's issue, was wonderfully instruc- tive. Your correspondent is evidently a faddist, and no one need go beyond his letter if they want to find the biassed way of looking at things, and the narrow and intolerant prejudices which have brought so many admirable schemes into contempt in this country: The particular fad of which Mr. Rethbone is the exponent is clearly that which finds embodiment in the Peace Society, a society which, without doubt, has done more to bring down unmerited scorn and obloquy on peace doctrines than any other agency in the three kingdoms. What is the Peace Society? It is a com- bination of party politicians whose special function it seems to be to find distinctions where no distinctions really exist, for party purposes. Its object, judging from its past I labours. is to prove that war is war witn a vengeance when waged by Tories, but thai when waged by Liberals it is something not quite so bad, only" military operations " or something of that kind. Who does not remember the sud- den access of piety and humanitarianism amongst the mem- bers of the Peace Society when the Tories were in office and engaged in war, and bow customary it was to turn up the white of the eye, to hold up the hands in pious horror. and to deprecate in sad humiliation the wrath of an offen- ded deity. But when Alex indria Wr9 bombarded, when Egyp- tians were slaughtered like sheep,and when naked Arabs were shot down in thousands with arms of precision, why then, I of course, it was a different thing. The name of the men Who ordered these things to be done was different. They were Liberals, the others were Tories, and this change by ' some strange and subtile alchemy altered the nature of the deeds. How is it that the Peace Society is treated with such scern and contumely, while the Md leaeae for the abolition of the Corn Laws is remembered with honour and respect? The answer is obvious. The one carried on its . propaganda and furthered in? object totally irrespective of . the convenience of any section or clique, while the other hae been degraded into the mere apologist and sub- servient inserument of a party. Although Mr. Rathbone is pleading for a cause which is entirely outside and above purely party or sectionel consi- derations, it is curious to note how his remarks are pervaded with a vein of partisan and class prejudice. Lord Salisbury, he admits, has "for once in his life" noise the truth. Why o for once ?" Does he mean to insinuate that Lord Salis- bury, the Prime Minister of the Britise Empire, and one of the ablest and most illustrious of Englishmen, is an invete- rate liar. Again, Mr. Hatt:bone would apparently have us to believe that wars have mainly been engaged in against the wish of the mass of the people, or, at all events, be- cause the people have not bad a sufficiently controlling voice in the management of national affairs. Now, nothing ceuld be more opposed to modern historical and contemporary fact than an assumption of this kind. So far as the history of the present century is concerned the very opposite conten- tion, that wars have been mainly engaged in because the rulers had not sufficient control over the people, would he nearer the truth. . Who is it that is to blame for tbe present strife in the Balkans, which may be fraught with such ter- rible issues, but the people of Serves., who titerelly drove Prince Milan into war ? What was the cause of the Russian attack on Turkey but the irrepsessible Sclavonic instinct of the Russian people? In France, what was it that hurled Napolecel to his fate but the tumultuous clamour of the. people of Paris? In our own country we have abundant instances in which the public desire for war has run far ahead of that of its rulers. Of the great " peace minister," William Pitt, one histories) says tieit "No hour of his life is so great as the hour when he stood alone in England and refused to bow to the growing cry of the nation for war;" and in the end he was compelled to yield, and that great war, or rather series of wars, which left us the legacy of our national debt was begun in obedience to popular pressure. Coming down to later times, no one can ta,e- that the Crimean war at its commencement was not a popular wa-, and with regard to the Chinese war—one of the most dis- graceful and ladefensible of wars—when Lord Palmerston asked for the opinion of the country, almost every promi- nent member of the peace party was ignominously rejected. My advice to Mr. Rathbone, and to all those who desire ta successfully preach doetrines and principles, is to shun party and class prejudices, and to net measures before mists. —I am. sir, HODGE,

Sir,—Will you allow me to correct a mi-r-tt-a-ie of Mr. Geo. Hazlehursr's at the meeting of the School Board, as re- ported in Tour last ? Mr. Hazlehurst said he thought the Board ought to consist ot three Churchmen, two Wesleyans, and one other Nonconformist, and one Roman Catholic, and added, " They had worked on these lines during the whole period of the Board's existence." The first Board consisted of four Nonconformists and three Churchmen, the members belt) ; Mr. Simister, Mi. Brookes, Mr. Pritchard, and my- self, Nonconformists; Canon Barclay, Mr. Briscoe, and Mr. Lea, Churchman. The HOITVIR Catholic vote was not sutH• eject to return a member. div.head: "THE KNIGHTS OF LABOUR."
div.p: "THE KNIGHTS OF LABOUR."

Sir,—ln your leader et Saturday, sth inst., on the order of "The Knights of Labour," you ray :—" The working- men of St. Helens, to the number of about 200, have joined the organisation." Now as this number is erroneoue, and the opening sentence of the paragraph is calculated to mis- lead the public as to what pat Ocular body of working-men 'have joined, please allow .2.-e to m.ke the following remarks : So far the St. Helens branch of this great labour association is purely composed of one particular branch of industry, viz., sheet or window glass workers solely, embracing blowers, gatherers, flatteners, and cutters. lustead of only 200 hav- ing joined, it has during the first year of its existence initiated 410 memeta, whose ranks are being proportionately augmented at the .e rapid rate of increase as prevails in any other glass making centre of Europe or the world. Eloping you will kindly insert this desirable correction in your next issue,—l am, sir, yours faithfully, JOSEPH NORBUIN, Secretary. Window Glees Workers' Universal Federation, St. Helens Branch. December Bth, 1885. Ormskirk-street.

Sir,—Allow me to congratulate the working-men of St. Helens in that they are taking up the lebour question in the creditable and useful manner I gather from your short leader. I know of ne reason wily they should not call themselves " Knights." As a distinctive title it is as good as any other, and all must allow that the associations of labour should be of good repute. Therefore I prefer " Knights of Labour " to' Trades Unionists." Previeue to the relied of Gr arge 111. it was no unusual thing for employers ard workmen to combine together, and for their mutual benefit, to enforce their rules upon all en- gaged in the same trades. By this action they checked un- healthy competitit-r, restricted tile system of apprenticeship, and, for a time, in a very narrow circle, brought about a "happy family "state of th!ngs. Sheffield was then the seat of England's hardware trades, and had, in a manner, a monopeiy, renowned throughout the world, for cutlery and edge tools, and as a consequence gradually nurtured the narrow Trade Union policy that caused so much misery a few year ago, and culminated in the Broadhead episode. While this was going on in Shef- field it was far different in the soft goods and other trades. The requirements of the people in other directions were manifold, and grew ta a surprising degree, causing trades to spring up in every town. Them not being willing to be tied down by any hard and fast rules, withdrew from association with their workmen, and, as a ccinsequence, we find first an evil system of competition sprung up ; this in its turn was helped forward .by an unreasonable placing of apprentices. In 1790, in Lane .shire, there were cases of tifty-five apprentices to two journeymen ; in Dumbarton sixty to two ; in other places similar. To make up.for un- skilfulness of boys, reduction of wages was resorted to. After this it is easy to see how neceesary it was for the workmen to combine; more especially when we note that employers were already in combination. Petitions in abundance flowed into Parliament in favour of the repeal of the combination laws. Of course these . were sturdily opposed by the employers, who alone had power in Parliament. Tory working-men might well consider the history of this particular period. Mr. Pitt, speaking on the subject of the Arbitration Act, said : "The time will Come wheel manufacturers will have been so long eetablished, and the operatives not having any other business to flee to, that it will be in the power ef any one man Pin a town to reduce the wages, and all other manufacturers will follow." The member for Warrington, Sir U. Greenall, told the present writer that he had invested £l,OOO in Longford Bridge Wire Works ; and no„ dispute in the wire trade has occurred within the past ten years without the wages paid at these works being given as a reason for reduction. To fight for the right to combine was no light task 100 years age. Men were seized on any trumped-up charge,' and in Sydney were sold into slavery at £l. per head. This ! has all been altered ; the reformers of those days, goaded I
on by the exectione of employer, never rafted until the

cornladnation laws were repealed, and now workmen have to reconsider their position. On the Continent and through- ' out Europe trade haa grown in a surprising degree. America, largely made up, in her populatien, tiy the most daring and enterprising spirits from Europe, bids fair ta take the trade of the world into her own hands. Protectior, which has male it possible for 15 persons ti own £lB4OOO 000. Pi now on its last legs. This being cleared away, her earn orting power will increase by " leaps and bounde." Then—what ? To effect this, and clear away the trammels, capital has surrounded itself with, and the workmen have formed them• selves into, trade unions. For years such a series of strikes have ensued as the world never before heard tell of. Not- withstanding the energetic action of the unions, wages have continued to decline, and now we read that America is not one whit behind other cnuntries in number of paupers or amount of misery. During the past four years wages have been reduced, on the average. 40 per cent. During the same period rents have risen fully 50 per cent, so that her industrial population is fast coming down to our own . level. The treat feature of trade unions has hitherto been a negative or resisting policy. Constructive or progressive ideas have seldom or never been taught. This is now found out to he a mistaka. Paying a weekly contribution into a Trade Union. under the cloak of paying it into a friendly society, and then expecting, with the help of the fund created, to successfully rbsist capital, is now proved to he mere chilli:Aloes., ending in nothing but a waste of energy and the complete demoralisation of workmen As in disputes between nations, so in disputes between employer anti employed, arbitration should be the first word mentioned. To rring this about in America the society of "Knights of Labour" has been formed, and your readers may like to know that in its declaration of principles the follow- ing passage occurs : "The alarming development and aggression of ea:m.oga- . .. . . . _ .

tel wealth, which, unless checked, will inevittbly lead to the panpsrisation and hopeless degradation of the toiling masses, renders it imp rative, if we desire to enjoy the Ides- ings of life, that a check should he placed upon its power ' and upon unjust accumulation' and a system adooted which will secure to the labourer the fruits of his tAI ; and, as this much-ilesired obj-ct can only be accsmplisbed by the thorough unifloation Oi those who labour, and the uni,ed efforts of those 'elm earn their bread by the sweat of their brow, we have formed the ' Order of the Knights of Lahatir,' with a view of securing the organisation an„d direction bv ! co-operative effort, of the power of the industrial classes ; and we submit to the world the objects sought to be 3CCOIII- - by our organis.ition, calling upon all who believe in secaring the `areatest good for the greatest number ' to aid and assist us."

In this long sentence several very important featnres oc- cur. Fist s.mi most important is the amalgamation of all trade s.eierlep. Ttla accomplished, the accumulation of wealth in the hands of a few, and the using of it aggres- sively, shrifd h., attended to. This can only he done satis. factotily by each union attending to its own trade, and b. leg well sustained by a confederation of unions. To acc,un-

lish this, the initiatory work m'ght well be taken up b.; the Trades Council. I see in your news column 3ou give s short report from the Warringt ,n Trades Council. Witt your permission I will in my next say a few word respec- ting this Council and its work. CLIFFORD DIX.

Mr. Spurgeon has left England for Mentone for rest and change ; he is very weak. The Earl of Warwick has made an abatement of fifteen per cent, in the rents of his Warwickshire tenantry, Three more arrests were made on Friday in conneclion with the recent overpowering and disarming of two police constables near Castle Island.
Many skaters who eluded the vigilance ef the police were immersed at St. James' Park on Friday. The water being shallow, no fatal results ensued.
The nuke of Devonshire returned ten per cent. to his tenants on his Chatsworth estate at the rent audit held at denser on Friday, besides making other material con- eeesions.

A Lloyds' telegram from Windau, dated Friday morning, says t—The English barque Kedron, bound for Riga with A cargo of dyeing wood, has stranded. The ship capsize, and the whole crew were drowned. At a sitting of the York Chancsry Court, on Friday morning, the Rev. Ja131051 Bell Cox, incumbent of St. Mar- caret's, Princes-road, Liverpool, was 2upended afi officio for six calendar months on account of Ritualistic prac- Cos.

_ _ The Queen, on Friday afternoon, with the Princa.qe Beatrice nail' a visit to the Duchess of Cambridge at St. James's Palaco. Her Majesty loft Windsor for London by special train at half-past four, returning to Windsor again about seven o'clock.

TITS SPEAKERSHIP.—It le stated that up to the preeent the Government have no intention of opposing the re-elec- tion of Mr. Peel to the Spealtership. The right hon. gentleman bag during the last few dare transacted business at the Speaker's residence.

Mr. Gladstone, acknowledging a letter from Dolgelly in- forming him that the Liberal victory in Merionethshire had been won under the leadership of sixty Nonconformist ministers, compliments the electors on their victory, and on the admirable conduct of the Nonconformist ministers. FATAL FIRE AT BIACKETTRN.—A. fire has broken not in the dwelling-bouae, No. 22, Pollard-street. Blackburn, oc- cupied by John Booth, weaver, but it was soon extinguished. Booth and his wife were out, but there were two children asie,p in bed. One of them, a boy aged two, was taken mitt dead through suffocation ; the other, a boy of dye years, was reacued before he had succumbed.

LIBEL ACTION AGAINST Tizttrm"—On Friday, in the Queen's Bench, Dublin, in the action brought by Alderman Harris against Mr. Labauchere, M.P , for alleged libels in Truth, charging the plaintiff with being A usurer, the Lord Chief Justice granted the defendant's application, compel- ling the plaintiff to answer interrogatories and make dis- covery of documents concerning his business. The case will not he tried till next sittings.

A LUMFD MURDER BY A MEDTCAL PRACTITIONER.— In the Queen's Bench Division, on Friday morning, counsel moved for a ruts calling upon the stipendiary magistrite at Birkenhead to show caut,o why bail should not be granted to Mr. do Tomanzie, now in Knutsford gaol, on the charge of murdering a woman. The ground of the application was that the orison-r might be enabled to collect evidence f, the defence. The Judge said the application was almost without prec.dent in the cane of and death. He would consider the matter, and announce his dedisionon Monday. . _

Public opinion will in time get rid of many ev of which w. now comrlain, and we might bur,len ourse/ves ton inur•h with legal reetricrions to suppress them. - —.— WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE —The monthly meeting of this body was held on Monday evening, in the Wesleyan School-room. An interesting programme was rendered, Meier& Kirk and Skilling taking the instrumental part. A pleasant evening was spent. CONGREGATIONAL CituncE.—Sermons in aid 'of the London Missionary Society will be preached in this church to-morrow (Sunday) and on Wednesday evening a public meeting will be held in the church in aid of the same object.

VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUTION. On Wedneeday evening the annual prize distribution of the Lymin Company of the 3rd Cheshire Rifle Voluuteers took place in the Drill Hall, Brookfield, Lymm, in the pre- I senor/ of the members of the Company and a number of visitors. The proceedings opened with a short speech from Captain Scott, who said that during the last year the Lvmm Company had been at the full strength permitt-d by Gov. ertiment, and had sent 96 men to camp for the whole week. The Company not only stood well in the Battalion for efficiency in drill, but also in shooting, some of the mem- bers having distinguished themselves in that respect. Their bugling had also become very good indeed. The Comp my awed a good deal to the lastructor, Sergeant McGarry. Due- -1 ing the time they were without en officer, Sergeant Mc- Garry had worked with them splendidly. He hoped that next year they would strive to maintain the position they had gained. The prizes were then distributed by Mr, G. B. Dewherst, J.P , who, in a few congratulatory remarks to the men, Spoke of the great importance of the volunteer service as a safeguard to the country in times of war, and as a means of rendering compulsory service unnecessary. After the distribution, Captain Moreland proposed a vote of thanks to the donors of prizes, which was seconded by Cap- tain Mothersill, supported by Captain Scott, and heartily carried,. A vote of thanks was also accorded to Mr. Dew- burst. During the proceedings a bayonet exercise competi- tion was decided, and music was played by the bend of the Battalion.

The prizes in money ranged from £2 to 2s 65, and were principally awarded with the tradesmen's prizes. The fol- lowing members of the corps took prizes:— i Colour-Sergeant W. Groves, Private J.
